Let $G_{\mathrm{acc}}$ have an edge $(x,L)$ exactly when $x\in L$ and $P_L(x)=f(x)$. If $\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\geq\varepsilon_*$ under uniform affine-line-then-point sampling, then $G_{\mathrm{acc}}$ contains a nonempty subgraph in which every point vertex has degree at least $407$ and every line vertex has degree at least $533$.
lemmas.title: Asymmetric pruning

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Every point lies on exactly $p+1$ affine lines, so double-counting point-line incidences gives

$$\sum_L n_L=(p+1)|X|.$$

The quantity $\sum_L n_L^2$ counts ordered pairs of points of $X$ lying on a common line. Each ordered pair of distinct points determines one line, while each diagonal pair lies on $p+1$ lines. Hence

$$\sum_L n_L^2=|X|(|X|-1)+(p+1)|X|=|X|^2+p|X|.$$

Since there are $p(p+1)$ affine lines,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_L\left(n_L-\frac{|X|}{p}\right)^2
&=|X|^2+p|X|-2\frac{|X|}{p}(p+1)|X|+p(p+1)\frac{|X|^2}{p^2}\\
&=p|X|-\frac{|X|^2}{p}\\
&=p^3a(1-a).
\end{aligned}
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. For $X\subseteq\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$, set $a:=|X|/p^2$ and $n_L:=|X\cap L|$ for every affine line $L$. Then

$$\sum_L\left(n_L-\frac{|X|}{p}\right)^2=p^3a(1-a).$$
lemmas.title: Centered line variance

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Write $\mathbf 1_T(L)$ for the indicator of $T$. Centering both factors gives

$$
\sum_L\bigl(\mathbf 1_T(L)-b\bigr)\left(n_L-\frac{|X|}{p}\right)
=|I(X,T)|-abp^2(p+1).
$$

The indicator variance is

$$\sum_L\bigl(\mathbf 1_T(L)-b\bigr)^2=p(p+1)b(1-b),$$

and the centered line-intersection variance is $p^3a(1-a)$ by the preceding variance identity. Cauchy-Schwarz therefore yields

$$
\left||I(X,T)|-abp^2(p+1)\right|
\leq p^2\sqrt{(p+1)a(1-a)b(1-b)}.
$$

Dividing by $p^2(p+1)$ proves the claimed bound without discarding either centered factor.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Let $X$ be a set of points and $T$ a set of affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$. Define

$$a:=\frac{|X|}{p^2},\qquad b:=\frac{|T|}{p(p+1)},$$

and

$$J(X,T):=\frac{|\{(x,L)\in X\times T:x\in L\}|}{p^2(p+1)}.$$

Then

$$|J(X,T)-ab|\leq\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}}.$$
lemmas.title: Centered incidence discrepancy

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set $e:=|E'|/N$. The minimum point and line degrees give

$$e\geq\alpha a,\qquad e\geq\beta b.$$

Every edge of $E'$ is an incidence between $X$ and $T$, so the centered incidence bound gives

$$e\leq ab+\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}}.$$

Suppose $a<\beta$. First assume $\alpha a\geq\beta b$. Then $b\leq ca<c\beta=\alpha<1/2$. Both $u$ and $\sqrt{u(1-u)}$ are increasing for $0\leq u<1/2$. Dividing the bounds by $a$ and substituting $b\leq ca$ therefore gives

$$
\alpha\leq ca+\sqrt{\frac{c(1-a)(1-ca)}{p+1}}.
$$

After division by $c$, and using $\alpha/c=\beta$ and $\gamma^2=1/(c(p+1))$, this becomes

$$\beta\leq a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.$$

Now assume $\beta b\geq\alpha a$. Then $b\geq ca$, $a/b\leq1/c$, and $1-b\leq1-ca$. Dividing by $b$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta
&\leq a+\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)(1-b)}{b(p+1)}}\\
&\leq a+\sqrt{\frac{(1-a)(1-ca)}{c(p+1)}}\\
&=a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two cases prove the conclusion.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Let $G_0$ be a nonempty accepted-incidence subgraph whose point degrees are at least $407$ and whose line degrees are at least $533$. Let $G=(X,T,E')$ be a connected component of $G_0$, and define

$$
N:=p^2(p+1),\quad a:=\frac{|X|}{p^2},\quad b:=\frac{|T|}{p(p+1)},
$$

$$
\alpha:=\frac{407}{147458},\quad
\beta:=\frac{533}{147457},\quad
c:=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}=\frac{60014999}{78595114},\quad
\gamma^2:=\frac{533}{407\cdot147457}=\frac{533}{60014999},
$$

and

$$\phi(z):=z+\gamma\sqrt{(1-z)(1-cz)}.$$

If $a<\beta$, then

$$\beta\leq\phi(a).$$
lemmas.title: Component density inequality

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For the fixed constants,

$$407\cdot533=216931>147457,$$

so $\beta>\gamma=\phi(0)$, while $\phi(\beta)>\beta$. Moreover,

$$\gamma^2<\frac1{100000}<\frac1{300^2},\qquad \beta<\frac1{200},\qquad c<1.$$

For $0\leq z\leq\beta$,

$$
\phi'(z)=1-\gamma\frac{(1+c)-2cz}{2\sqrt{(1-z)(1-cz)}}>0.
$$

Indeed, the fraction following $\gamma$ is less than $200/199$, whereas $\gamma<1/300$. Thus $\phi$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\beta]$ and has a unique $a_*\in(0,\beta)$ satisfying $\phi(a_*)=\beta$.

Set

$$T:=\frac{\varepsilon_*}{10}=\frac{20395544151487}{32062628804198420}.$$

Exact rational arithmetic gives

$$\beta-T=\frac{95498453099493}{32062628804198420}>0$$

and

$$
(\beta-T)^2-\gamma^2(1-T)(1-cT)
=\frac{11162676738358540618967673}{38036708085362154141370285169079200}>0.
$$

Consequently,

$$T+\gamma\sqrt{(1-T)(1-cT)}<\beta,$$

so $\phi(T)<\beta=\phi(a_*)$ and hence $T<a_*$. If $a\geq\beta$, then $a>T$. If $a<\beta$, the component density inequality gives $\beta\leq\phi(a)$, whence strict monotonicity gives $a\geq a_*>T$. Thus every component has $a>\varepsilon_*/10$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, and set

$$\varepsilon_*:=\frac{20395544151487}{3206262880419842}.$$

Let $G_0$ be a nonempty accepted-incidence subgraph whose point degrees are at least $407$ and whose line degrees are at least $533$. If $X$ is the point set of any connected component of $G_0$, then

$$\frac{|X|}{147457^2}>\frac{\varepsilon_*}{10}.$$
lemmas.title: Component threshold

lemmas.proof_markdown:
With $T:=\varepsilon_*/10$,

$$
Tp^2=\frac{20395544151487}{1474580}
=13831426+\frac{407}{1474580}.
$$

The strict density bound gives $|X|>Tp^2$. Since $|X|$ is an integer, $|X|\geq13831427$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, and set

$$\varepsilon_*:=\frac{20395544151487}{3206262880419842}.$$

Let $G_0$ be a nonempty accepted-incidence subgraph whose point degrees are at least $407$ and whose line degrees are at least $533$. If $X$ is the point set of any connected component of $G_0$, then

$$|X|\geq13831427.$$
lemmas.title: Integral component size

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose a point vertex $b=(b_1,b_2)$ and put $z_0:=f(b)$. Since $B_Z(b_1,b_2,z_0)\neq0$, formal implicit lifting at this simple root constructs the unique total-degree-at-most-$87$ truncation $Q$ with $Q(b)=z_0$ and

$$B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0\pmod{\mathfrak m_b^{88}},$$

where $\mathfrak m_b=(X-b_1,Y-b_2)$. The coefficient recursion divides only by the explicitly nonzero scalar $B_Z(b_1,b_2,z_0)$.

Reparametrize each graph line through $b$ so that $L(0)=b$. The restrictions $Q(L(t))$ and $P_L(t)$ have degree at most $87$, have the same constant term, and are the same simple-root lift through order $87$. Univariate lift uniqueness therefore gives

$$Q(L(t))=P_L(t)$$

for each of the at least $407$ graph lines through $b$.

Set

$$R(X,Y):=B(X,Y,Q(X,Y)).$$

The weighted-degree bound on $B$ and the total-degree bound on $Q$ imply $\deg R\leq406$. The polynomial $R$ vanishes identically on at least $407$ distinct affine lines through $b$. Their distinct linear equations would have a product of degree $407$ dividing a nonzero $R$, which is impossible. Hence $R=0$.

Suppose a component line $L$ has already been reached and $Q|_L=P_L$. At every adjacent accepted point $x$, one has $Q(x)=P_L(x)=f(x)$. Since $B_Z(x_1,x_2,f(x))\neq0$, the restrictions of $Q$ and every adjacent $P_{L'}$ are the same one-variable simple-root branch at $x$. Univariate uniqueness gives $Q|_{L'}=P_{L'}$. Alternating this argument across point and line vertices and using connectivity proves all asserted equalities.

All lifting identities are formal. Since $87,406<147457$, the argument uses no high-degree polynomial-function identification; its only field division is by a stated nonzero value of $B_Z$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Let $G=(\mathcal X,\mathcal T,E)$ be a connected accepted-incidence graph in $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$ whose point vertices have degree at least $407$. Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb F_{147457}$, and for each $L\in\mathcal T$ fix an affine parametrization $L(t)=(L_1(t),L_2(t))$ and a polynomial $P_L(t)$ of degree at most $87$. Suppose every edge $(x,L)\in E$ satisfies $x=L(t_x)$ and $P_L(t_x)=f(x)$ for the corresponding parameter $t_x$.

Let $B\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ have $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $406$. Suppose that, with $B_Z:=\partial B/\partial Z$,

$$B(x_1,x_2,f(x))=0\quad\text{and}\quad B_Z(x_1,x_2,f(x))\neq0$$

for every $x=(x_1,x_2)\in\mathcal X$, and

$$B(L_1(t),L_2(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$$

for every $L\in\mathcal T$. Then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that

$$Q(x_1,x_2)=f(x)$$

for every $x\in\mathcal X$, and

$$Q(L_1(t),L_2(t))=P_L(t)$$

for every $L\in\mathcal T$.
lemmas.title: Curve propagation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose $407$ distinct incident line vertices at $b$. A monomial $X^iY^jZ^k$ has admissible weight when

$$i+j+87k\leq406.$$

Thus the dimension of the space of admissible polynomials is

$$
\binom{408}{2}+\binom{321}{2}+\binom{234}{2}+\binom{147}{2}+\binom{60}{2}
=83028+51360+27261+10731+1770
=174150.
$$

For each selected line, substituting $L_1(t)$, $L_2(t)$, and $P_L(t)$ produces a univariate polynomial of degree at most $406$. Its identical vanishing imposes at most $407$ homogeneous linear conditions. The $407$ line identities therefore impose at most

$$407^2=165649<174150$$

conditions, so a nonzero relation exists.

Such a relation must depend on $Z$. Otherwise it would be a nonzero bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $406$ vanishing identically on $407$ distinct geometric lines through $b$, which is impossible.

Replace the relation by the product of its distinct irreducible factors. This squarefree radical has no larger weighted degree. For each selected line, at least one factor of the original relation vanishes after substitution, so the radical still vanishes on that line graph. It also still depends on $Z$. Finally,

$$\deg_Z B\leq\left\lfloor\frac{406}{87}\right\rfloor=4<147457.$$

Because $B$ depends on $Z$ and every positive $Z$-exponent is smaller than the characteristic, its formal derivative $B_Z$ is not the zero polynomial.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Let $b$ be a point vertex of degree at least $407$ in an accepted-incidence graph over $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$, and let each incident line vertex $L$ carry a polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$. Then there exist $407$ distinct incident line vertices $\mathcal L_b$ and a nonzero polynomial $B\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $406$ such that

$$B(L_1(t),L_2(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$$

for every $L\in\mathcal L_b$, and

$$\frac{\partial B}{\partial Z}\not\equiv0.$$
lemmas.title: Local weighted interpolation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The local interpolation step constructs a relation separately at each core point and only for $407$ selected incident line graphs. It does not show that a single relation, or a single factor of such a relation, governs every line graph in one connected component. It also proves only that the formal derivative with respect to $Z$ is a nonzero polynomial; it does not prove that

$$B_Z(x_1,x_2,f(x))\neq0$$

at every required point vertex. Hence the component-wide identities and pointwise simple-root conditions in the statement have not been derived from acceptance alone. If both properties were established without lowering the core degrees, the curve-propagation lemma would apply. The displayed claim therefore remains conditional.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, and set

$$\varepsilon_*:=\frac{20395544151487}{3206262880419842}.$$

Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and let every affine line $L$ carry a polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$. If $\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\geq\varepsilon_*$, then there exist a connected accepted-incidence subgraph $G=(\mathcal X,\mathcal T,E)$ with minimum point degree at least $407$ and minimum line degree at least $533$, and a nonzero polynomial $B\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $406$, such that

$$B(x_1,x_2,f(x))=0\quad\text{and}\quad B_Z(x_1,x_2,f(x))\neq0$$

for every $x=(x_1,x_2)\in\mathcal X$, and

$$B(L_1(t),L_2(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$$

for every $L\in\mathcal T$.
lemmas.title: Component-wide relation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The vector space of bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$ has dimension

$$\binom{89}{2}=3916,$$

so there are at most $p^{3916}$ candidates. Choose the values $f(x)$ independently and uniformly in $\mathbb F_p$. For a fixed candidate $Q$, its agreement count with $f$ has distribution $\operatorname{Bin}(p^2,1/p)$ and mean $p$. The moment bound gives

$$\Pr\bigl[|\{x:Q(x)=f(x)\}|\geq2p\bigr]\leq\left(\frac e4\right)^p<\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^p.$$

Since

$$p<2^{18},\qquad \left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^2<\frac12,\qquad p=2\cdot73728+1,$$

and

$$18\cdot3916=70488<73728,$$

the union probability over all candidates is less than

$$2^{70488-73728}<1.$$

Thus some table $f$ agrees with every degree-at-most-$87$ bivariate polynomial on at most $2p-1$ points.

On each affine line, choose $88=d+1$ distinct points and interpolate the values of $f$ there by a univariate polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$. This is valid because $88<147457$, so all Vandermonde denominators are nonzero. Each line has at least $88$ accepted points, and hence

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\geq\frac{88}{p}.$$

For the chosen $f$,

$$
\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)
\leq\frac{2p-1}{p^2}
<\frac2p
<\frac{88}{10p}.
$$

This probabilistic-method argument proves the asserted witness.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Define

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f):=\max_{\deg Q\leq87}\frac{|\{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}:Q(x)=f(x)\}|}{147457^2},$$

where the maximum is over bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$. There exist a table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and degree-at-most-$87$ line polynomials $(P_L)_L$ such that

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\geq\frac{88}{147457}$$

and

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<\frac{2}{147457}<\frac{88}{10\cdot147457}.$$
lemmas.title: Random-table obstruction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Every point of $\mathbb F_p^2$ lies on exactly one line in each of the $p+1$ directions. For lines in $\mathcal D$, the constant-zero polynomial agrees with $f$ at all $p$ points; for every other line, the constant-one polynomial agrees nowhere. Consequently, every point has exactly $939$ accepted incident lines, and the accepted lines are precisely the lines in the selected directions. Since every direction contains $p$ parallel lines,

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac{939p}{p(p+1)}=\frac{939}{147458}.$$

Moreover,

$$939p^2=20417209271211>20395544151487,$$

so

$$\frac{939}{147458}>\frac{20395544151487}{p^2(p+1)}=\varepsilon_*.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, and set

$$\varepsilon_*:=\frac{20395544151487}{3206262880419842}.$$

Let $\mathcal D$ be any set of $939$ affine-line directions in $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$. Define $f(x):=0$ for every point and

$$
P_L:=
\begin{cases}
0,&\text{if the direction of }L\text{ lies in }\mathcal D,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Then

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac{939}{147458}>\varepsilon_*,$$

and every point has accepted degree exactly $939$.
lemmas.title: Direction concentration

lemmas.proof_markdown:
There are $p+1$ incidences between $X$ and $T$. Hence

$$a=\frac1{p^2},\qquad b=\frac1p,\qquad J(X,T)=\frac{p+1}{p^2(p+1)}=\frac1{p^2}.$$

Therefore

$$J(X,T)-ab=\frac1{p^2}-\frac1{p^3}=\frac{p-1}{p^3}.$$

Also,

$$
\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}
=\frac{(p-1)^2}{p^6},
$$

so its square root is $(p-1)/p^3$. This gives equality in the centered incidence bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Fix $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$. Let $X$ consist of one point of $\mathbb F_{147457}^{2}$, and let $T$ be the pencil of all $p+1$ affine lines through that point. Define

$$a:=\frac{|X|}{p^2},\qquad b:=\frac{|T|}{p(p+1)},$$

and

$$J(X,T):=\frac{|\{(x,L)\in X\times T:x\in L\}|}{p^2(p+1)}.$$

Then

$$J(X,T)-ab=\frac{p-1}{p^3}=\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}}.$$
lemmas.title: Pencil extremizer

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Since $87668=87\cdot1007+59$, every exponent $k$ occurring in $V_D$ satisfies $k\le 1007<147457$. Thus characteristic pruning removes no monomial. Reversing the summation index gives

$$\dim V_D=\sum_{k=0}^{1007}\binom{87668-87k+2}{2}=\sum_{j=0}^{1007}\binom{87j+61}{2}.$$

Using

$$\sum_{j=0}^{1007}1=1008,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{1007}j=507528,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{1007}j^2=340889640,$$

we obtain

$$\dim V_D=\frac{7569(340889640)+10527(507528)+3660(1008)}{2}=1292770060848.$$

Substituting an affine parametrization and a polynomial of degree at most $87$ into a monomial of weighted degree at most $D$ produces a univariate polynomial of degree at most $D$. Each line identity therefore imposes at most $D+1=87669$ homogeneous linear conditions. Hence

$$\operatorname{rank}\Phi\le 14745800\cdot87669=1292749540200.$$

Rank-nullity yields

$$\dim\ker\Phi\ge1292770060848-1292749540200=20520648.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, $d=87$, $D=87668$, and $r_0=100(p+1)=14745800$. Define

$$V_D=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_{147457}}\left\{X^iY^jZ^k:i,j,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ i+j+87k\le D\right\}.$$

For every set $R$ of $r_0$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$, every choice of affine parametrizations $L(t)$, and every family $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$, let

$$\Phi:V_D\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{L\in R}\mathbb F_{147457}[t]_{\le D},\qquad \Phi(A)=\bigl(A(L(t),p_L(t))\bigr)_{L\in R}.$$

Then

$$\dim V_D=1292770060848>1292749540200=r_0(D+1)$$

and

$$\dim\ker\Phi\ge20520648.$$
lemmas.title: Weighted monomial space

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The plane $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ has

$$147457(147457+1)=21743714306>14745800$$

affine lines. If $|R|<14745800$, augment $R$ to a set $R'$ of exactly $14745800$ distinct affine lines and assign an arbitrary degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial label to each added line. The weighted-monomial count gives a kernel of dimension at least $20520648$ for the resulting restriction map. Any nonzero element $A$ of this kernel has weighted degree at most $87668$ and satisfies every formal identity indexed by $R'$. Discarding the added lines leaves all identities indexed by $R$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$. Let $R$ be a set of at most $14745800$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. For every $L\in R$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$. Then there exists a nonzero polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le87668$$

and, for every $L\in R$,

$$A(L(t),p_L(t))=0\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t].$$
lemmas.title: Fixed-instance interpolant

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Augment $R$ to a set $R'$ of exactly $14745800$ distinct affine lines and assign arbitrary degree-at-most-$87$ labels to the added lines. The interpolation lemma supplies a nonzero interpolant $A$ for $R'$.

Suppose that $A$ is independent of $Z$. For every $L\in R'$, the formal identity $A(L(t))=0$ implies that the affine-linear defining polynomial $\ell_L$ of $L$ divides $A$. Distinct affine lines have nonassociate irreducible defining polynomials, so

$$\prod_{L\in R'}\ell_L\mid A.$$

Consequently,

$$\deg A\ge |R'|=14745800,$$

contrary to $\deg A\le87668$. Thus $A$ depends on $Z$.

Every positive exponent $k$ of $Z$ in $A$ satisfies

$$1\le k\le\left\lfloor\frac{87668}{87}\right\rfloor=1007<147457.$$

Its derivative coefficient is therefore nonzero in $\mathbb F_{147457}$, and distinct monomials remain distinct after differentiation. Hence $A_Z\ne0$. Restricting the identities from $R'$ to $R$ proves the claim.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$. Let $R$ be a set of at most $14745800$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. For every $L\in R$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$. Then there exists a nonzero polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le87668,\qquad A_Z\ne0,$$

and, for every $L\in R$,

$$A(L(t),p_L(t))=0\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t].$$
lemmas.title: Formal differentiation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose, among the interpolants supplied by the preceding lemma with nonzero $Z$-derivative, a polynomial $A$ of minimum weighted degree. Suppose that $A$ has a repeated irreducible factor, and write

$$A=F^eG,$$

where $F$ is irreducible, $e\ge2$, and $F\nmid G$. For each $L\in R$, set

$$F_L(t)=F(L(t),p_L(t)),\qquad G_L(t)=G(L(t),p_L(t)).$$

The identity $F_L^eG_L=0$ holds in the integral domain $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$. Thus either $F_L=0$ or $G_L=0$, and consequently $F_LG_L=0$. Therefore $B=FG$ remains an interpolant.

Suppose that $B_Z=0$. Then

$$F_ZG+FG_Z=0.$$

Reduction modulo $F$ gives $F\mid F_ZG$. Since the polynomial ring is a unique factorization domain, $F$ is prime; because $F\nmid G$, it follows that $F\mid F_Z$. If $F_Z\ne0$, then $\deg_Z(F_Z)<\deg_Z(F)$, which is incompatible with this divisibility. Hence $F_Z=0$. The equality $B_Z=0$ then gives $G_Z=0$, and therefore

$$A_Z=eF^{e-1}F_ZG+F^eG_Z=0,$$

contrary to the choice of $A$. Thus $B_Z\ne0$.

Weighted degree is additive on products of nonzero polynomials. Since $F$ is nonconstant and $e\ge2$,

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)<\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A),$$

contradicting minimality. Hence $A$ has no repeated irreducible factor and is squarefree.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$. Let $R$ be a set of at most $14745800$ distinct affine lines in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. For every $L\in R$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and a polynomial $p_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg p_L\le87$. Then there exists a nonzero squarefree polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that

$$\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le87668,\qquad A_Z\ne0,$$

and, for every $L\in R$,

$$A(L(t),p_L(t))=0\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t].$$
lemmas.title: Squarefree reduction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The inequality holds at $D=87668$ by the exact count in the weighted-monomial lemma. At $D=87667$,

$$N(D)=1292725845432,$$

whereas

$$14745800(D+1)=14745800\cdot87668=1292734794400.$$

The deficit is $8948968$.

Let $a_s$ be the number of supported monomials of exact weighted degree $s$. Multiplication by $X$ injects the layer of weight $s$ into the layer of weight $s+1$, so $(a_s)_{s\ge0}$ is nondecreasing. Consequently,

$$\frac{N(E)}{E+1}=\frac{1}{E+1}\sum_{s=0}^{E}a_s$$

is nondecreasing in $E$. For every $E\le87667$,

$$\frac{N(E)}{E+1}\le\frac{N(87667)}{87668}<14745800.$$

Thus no smaller degree satisfies the universal coefficient-count inequality. This establishes optimality only for that certificate; it does not rule out smaller interpolants for particular labeled-line data.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For $D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, define

$$N(D)=\#\left\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:i+j+87k\le D,\ k=0\text{ or }147457\nmid k\right\}.$$

Then

$$\min\left\{D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:N(D)>14745800(D+1)\right\}=87668.$$
lemmas.title: Coefficient-count threshold

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Exact counting at $d=87$ and $D=8700$ gives

$$\left|\mathcal N_{87,8700}\right|=\sum_{j=0}^{100}\binom{87j+2}{2}=1281144701.$$

The asserted lower bound evaluates to

$$\frac{8700^3}{3\cdot87}-\frac{5}{2}8700^2+\frac{8700\cdot87}{6}=2333901150.$$

This exceeds the exact count by $1052756449$. Hence the displayed inequality, and therefore HKSS v1 Claim A.4 as printed, is false at this specialization.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For positive integers $d$ and $D$, define

$$\mathcal N_{d,D}=\left\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:i+j+dk\le D\right\}.$$

At $d=87$ and $D=8700$,

$$\left|\mathcal N_{87,8700}\right|\ge\frac{8700^3}{3\cdot87}-\frac{5}{2}8700^2+\frac{8700\cdot87}{6}.$$
lemmas.title: HKSS specialization

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Let $q=\lfloor D/d\rfloor$, and let $\mathcal N_{d,D}$ denote the same set without the restriction on $k$. Then

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|=\sum_{k=0}^{q}\binom{D-dk+2}{2}\ge\frac12\sum_{k=0}^{q}(D-dk)^2.$$

The function $x\mapsto(D-dx)^2$ is nonnegative and decreasing on $[0,D/d]$. Therefore

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|\ge\frac12\int_0^{D/d}(D-dx)^2\,dx=\frac{D^3}{6d}.$$

Group the positive $Z$-exponents into blocks

$$\{ap+1,\ldots,(a+1)p\},\qquad a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$$

Within every complete block, the excluded exponent $(a+1)p$ has the smallest monomial layer, so its contribution is at most $1/p$ of the block's contribution. A terminal incomplete block contains no excluded exponent, and the layer $k=0$ is retained. Hence

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D,p}\right|\ge\left(1-\frac1p\right)\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|\ge\frac12\left|\mathcal N_{d,D}\right|\ge\frac{D^3}{12d}.$$

This proof does not use the refuted HKSS lower bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For $d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}$, $D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and a prime $p\ge2$, define

$$\mathcal N_{d,D,p}=\left\{(i,j,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^3:i+j+dk\le D,\ k=0\text{ or }p\nmid k\right\}.$$

Then

$$\left|\mathcal N_{d,D,p}\right|\ge\frac{D^3}{12d}.$$
lemmas.title: Characteristic-pruned count

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set

$$r_0=100(p+1)=14745800.$$

Then

$$87r_0=1282884600$$

and

$$35817^2=1282857489<87r_0<1282929124=35818^2.$$

The prescribed KTZ degree is therefore

$$16\left(\left\lfloor\sqrt{87r_0}\right\rfloor+1\right)=16(35817+1)=573088>147457.$$

Exact coefficient counting instead permits $D=87668<147457$, but the later requirements still fail. For every $0<\epsilon\le1$, let

$$k_1=\left\lfloor\frac{\epsilon p}{1000}\right\rfloor.$$

Then $k_1\le147$, so $D<k_1/2$ forces the integer $D\le73$. Any polynomial with $A_Z\ne0$ under the $(1,1,87)$ weighting has weighted degree at least $87$, which is incompatible with this requirement.

Moreover,

$$384^2<p+1<385^2,$$

so

$$\frac1{\sqrt{p+1}}>\frac1{385}>\frac1{8000}\ge\frac{\epsilon}{8000}.$$

Thus the required mixing inequality $1/\sqrt{p+1}\le\epsilon/8000$ also fails for every $0<\epsilon\le1$. Finally, the printed recovery bound $\epsilon/8000$ is weaker than the required bound $\epsilon/10$. Hence the printed fixed-instance slack chain cannot be instantiated. This does not refute the asymptotic KTZ theorem.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, the printed explicit KTZ slack chain can be instantiated.
lemmas.title: KTZ slack specialization

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set $p=147457$. By the pigeonhole principle, some $a\in\mathbb F_p$ satisfies

$$\left|\left\{x\in\mathbb F_p^2:f(x)=a\right\}\right|\ge\frac{p^2}{p}=p.$$

The constant polynomial $Q(X,Y)=a$ has total degree $0$, and

$$\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_p^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]\ge\frac{p}{p^2}=\frac1{147457}>\frac1{10000000}=10^{-7}.$$

The hypothesis $\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge10^{-6}$ is unused, so the conclusion holds independently of acceptance.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ be a point table, and let $P$ assign to every affine line a univariate polynomial of degree at most $87$. If

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge10^{-6},$$

then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that

$$\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]\ge10^{-7}.$$
lemmas.title: Constant-polynomial agreement

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set $p=147457$. The number of monomials $X^iY^j$ with $i+j\le87$ is

$$\binom{89}{2}=3916.$$

Consequently, there are at most $p^{3916}$ bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$. Choose every value $f(x)$ independently and uniformly from $\mathbb F_p$. For a fixed polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$, let

$$X_Q=\left|\left\{x\in\mathbb F_p^2:Q(x)=f(x)\right\}\right|.$$

Then $X_Q$ is binomial with parameters $p^2$ and $1/p$, and

$$\mathbb E[2^{X_Q}]=\left(1-\frac1p+\frac2p\right)^{p^2}=\left(1+\frac1p\right)^{p^2}.$$

Markov's inequality gives

$$\Pr[X_Q\ge2p]\le\frac{(1+1/p)^{p^2}}{4^p}.$$

The standard exponential estimate gives $(1+1/p)^p<e$. Moreover,

$$e\le1+1+\frac12+\frac16+\frac1{24}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}4^{-j}=\frac{49}{18}<\frac{11}{4}.$$

It follows that

$$\Pr[X_Q\ge2p]<\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^p.$$

Taking a union bound over all eligible $Q$ gives

$$\Pr[\exists Q:X_Q\ge2p]<p^{3916}\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^p.$$

Since

$$p<2^{18},\qquad p=2\cdot73728+1,\qquad \left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^2<\frac12,$$

we have

$$p^{3916}\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^p<2^{18\cdot3916-73728}=2^{-3240}<1.$$

Thus some deterministic $f$ satisfies $X_Q<2p$ for every polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$. For this table,

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)=\max_{\deg Q\le87}\frac{X_Q}{p^2}<\frac{2p}{p^2}=\frac2{147457}.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
There exists a point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ such that

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<\frac2{147457}.$$
lemmas.title: Random point table

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose a point table $f$ supplied by the preceding lemma and set $p=147457$. For every affine line $L$, fix an affine parametrization $L(t)$ and choose distinct elements

$$t_{L,1},\ldots,t_{L,88}\in\mathbb F_p.$$

This is possible because $88<p$. Define

$$P_L(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{88}f(L(t_{L,i}))\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le88\\j\ne i}}\frac{t-t_{L,j}}{t_{L,i}-t_{L,j}}.$$

All denominators are nonzero, and $P_L$ has degree at most $87$. It agrees with $f$ at the selected $88$ points of $L$. Under uniform line-then-point sampling,

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac1{p(p+1)}\sum_L\frac{\left|\left\{t\in\mathbb F_p:P_L(t)=f(L(t))\right\}\right|}{p}\ge\frac{88}{p}.$$

The choice of $f$ also gives $\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<2/p$. For every $\epsilon$ with $20/p\le\epsilon\le88/p$,

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge\frac{88}{p}\ge\epsilon$$

and

$$\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<\frac2p\le\frac{\epsilon}{10}.$$

Thus the target implication is refuted throughout the stated interval.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
There exist a point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and a line table $P$, assigning a polynomial of degree at most $87$ to every affine line, such that

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge\frac{88}{147457}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<\frac2{147457}.$$

For every

$$\epsilon\in\left[\frac{20}{147457},\frac{88}{147457}\right],$$

the same tables satisfy

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge\epsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)<\frac{\epsilon}{10}.$$
lemmas.title: Linewise interpolation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $p=147457$ and $\Lambda=p(p+1)=21743714306$. Normalize edge counts by the total number $p\Lambda$ of point-line incidences. Charge each deleted edge when its first endpoint is removed. A deleted point has current degree at most $31626$, so all point deletions remove normalized edge measure at most

$$
\frac{p^2\cdot31626}{p\Lambda}
=\frac{31626}{p+1}
=\frac{4663475082}{\Lambda}.
$$

A deleted line has current degree at most $38341$, so all line deletions remove normalized edge measure at most

$$
\frac{\Lambda\cdot38341}{p\Lambda}
=\frac{38341}{p}
=\frac{5653687178}{\Lambda}.
$$

Every removed edge is charged once. Hence the total normalized loss is at most

$$
\frac{4663475082+5653687178}{21743714306}
=\frac{10317162260}{21743714306}.
$$

When deletion terminates, any remaining point has degree at least $31627$, and any remaining line has degree at least $38342$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G$ be an accepted incidence graph between the points of $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ and its affine lines. Starting from $G$, alternately delete any point vertex of current degree below $31627$ and any line vertex of current degree below $38342$ until neither deletion applies. The normalized edge measure removed is at most $\frac{10317162260}{21743714306}$. If the resulting graph is nonempty, every remaining point has degree at least $31627$ and every remaining line has degree at least $38342$.
lemmas.title: First-Core Pruning

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Every accepted point neighbor $x$ of $L$ has degree at least $31627$ in $G_1$, so at least $31626$ lines of $G_1$ other than $L$ pass through $x$. With $\theta=1/79065$,

$$
31626\theta=\frac{31626}{79065}=\frac25.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\Pr[I_x=1]
\ge 1-(1-\theta)^{31626}
>1-e^{-2/5}.
$$

The exact exponential-series calculation

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{6}\frac{(2/5)^j}{j!}
=\frac{1048939}{703125}
$$

and the cross-product identity

$$
1048939\cdot67033-100000\cdot703125
=1027987>0
$$

show that $e^{2/5}>100000/67033$. Thus

$$
1-e^{-2/5}>1-\frac{67033}{100000}
=\frac{32967}{100000}.
$$

If $x$ and $y$ are distinct points of $L$, no affine line other than $L$ passes through both. Their sets of alternative lines are therefore disjoint, so the indicators $I_x$ and $I_y$ are independent. Coupling each independent indicator with an independent Bernoulli variable of parameter $32967/100000$ gives the asserted stochastic domination.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_1$ be a nonempty first core furnished by $P1$. Independently select each line vertex of $G_1$ with probability $\theta=1/79065$. For a line $L$ of $G_1$ and an accepted point neighbor $x$ of $L$, let $I_x$ indicate that a selected line of $G_1$ distinct from $L$ passes through $x$. Then the family $(I_x)_{x\in N_{G_1}(L)}$ stochastically dominates a family of independent Bernoulli variables of parameter $32967/100000$.
lemmas.title: Alternative-Line Coverage

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Set

$$
n=38342,
\qquad
\rho=\frac{32967}{100000},
\qquad
a_0=\frac{11919}{38342},
\qquad
x=\rho-a_0=\frac{36060357}{1917100000}.
$$

For $0<x<\rho<1/2$, the Bernoulli relative entropy has the positive expansion

$$
K(\rho-x\mathbin\Vert\rho)
=\sum_{j\ge2}\frac{x^j}{j(j-1)}
\left(\rho^{1-j}+(-1)^j(1-\rho)^{1-j}\right).
$$

Keeping the terms with $j=2,3,4$ gives $K_4$, for which

$$
38342K_4
=31+
\frac{15263601856608908791454208929273506651}
{5632546505820224973227839313525458959966}
>31.
$$

The Chernoff bound therefore yields

$$
\Pr\left[\operatorname{Bin}(38342,\rho)\le11919\right]<e^{-31}.
$$

The domination from $P2$ gives the same failure bound for every first-core line, including lines with more than $38342$ accepted neighbors. Put $\Lambda=21743714306$. The exact comparisons

$$
10\cdot1957^7-10959\cdot720^7
=94611698058600748930>0,
$$

$$
25\cdot1957^3-502\cdot720^3
=4866325>0,
$$

and

$$
751\cdot502\cdot10959^4
-10^6\cdot\Lambda\cdot250000
=1923154232516500522>0
$$

imply

$$
\Lambda e^{-31}<\frac{751}{10^6}.
$$

Thus the event $E$ that every first-core line has at least $11920$ covered accepted neighbors has probability greater than $999249/10^6$.

For the randomly selected family $R$,

$$
\mathbb E|R|\le\frac{\Lambda}{79065}.
$$

Moreover,

$$
275218\cdot79065\cdot999249
-\Lambda\cdot10^6
=55020511330>0.
$$

Hence $\mathbb E[|R|\mid E]<275218$. Some outcome in $E$ therefore has the integer size $|R|\le275217$. It has the required coverage property. Distinct covered points of a fixed line require distinct selected alternative lines, so this outcome also satisfies $|R|\ge11920>11919$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_1$ be a first core. There exists a set $R$ of at most $275217$ line vertices of $G_1$ such that every line vertex $L$ of $G_1$ has at least $11920$ accepted point neighbors, each incident to a line in $R\setminus\{L\}$.
lemmas.title: Selected-Line Family

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Consider the weighted interpolation space

$$
V_{11919}
=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_{147457}}
\left\{X^iY^jZ^k:i,j,k\ge0,\ i+j+87k\le11919\right\}.
$$

Since $11919=87\cdot137$,

$$
\dim V_{11919}
=\sum_{k=0}^{137}\binom{11919-87k+2}{2}
=\sum_{j=0}^{137}\binom{87j+2}{2}
=3280597617.
$$

After substituting an affine parametrization of $L$ and a label $P_L$ of degree at most $87$, every monomial of weighted degree at most $11919$ becomes a univariate polynomial of degree at most $11919$. The identity $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ therefore imposes at most $11920$ homogeneous linear equations. Since

$$
275217\cdot11920=3280586640,
$$

the coefficient surplus is

$$
3280597617-3280586640=10977>0.
$$

Rank-nullity supplies a nonzero interpolant $A\in V_{11919}$.

By $P3$, the selected family has at least $11920>11919$ distinct lines. If $A$ were independent of $Z$, it would be a nonzero bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $11919$ vanishing identically on more than $11919$ affine lines, which is impossible. Hence $A$ genuinely depends on $Z$. Every positive $Z$-exponent in $A$ is at most

$$
\left\lfloor\frac{11919}{87}\right\rfloor=137<147457.
$$

No such exponent vanishes in the characteristic of $\mathbb F_{147457}$ under differentiation, so $A_Z\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For every line family $R$ furnished by $P3$ and every assignment of a univariate polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$ to each $L\in R$, there exists a nonzero polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ of weighted degree at most $11919$ for weights $(1,1,87)$ such that $A_Z\ne0$ and $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every $L\in R$.
lemmas.title: Weighted Interpolant

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose from the interpolants in $\mathcal A$ one having minimum weighted degree. Suppose it has a repeated irreducible factor, and write

$$
A=F^eG,
\qquad e\ge2,
\qquad F\nmid G.
$$

For every selected line $L\in R$, the identity

$$
F_L^eG_L=0
$$

holds in the integral domain $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$. Hence $F_LG_L=0$, so $FG$ still vanishes on every selected labeled line graph. If $(FG)_Z=0$, then reduction modulo $F$ gives $F\mid F_ZG$. Since $F\nmid G$, this implies $F\mid F_Z$, and therefore $F_Z=0$. The equality $(FG)_Z=0$ then gives $G_Z=0$, which would imply $A_Z=0$, a contradiction. Thus $(FG)_Z\ne0$. Since $FG$ has smaller weighted degree than $A$, it belongs to $\mathcal A$ and contradicts minimality. Therefore $A$ is squarefree.

Now let $L$ be any line of the first core. By $P3$, it has at least $11920$ distinct covered accepted points. At each such point $x$, some selected alternative line $M\in R$ passes through $x$, and

$$
P_L(x)=f(x)=P_M(x).
$$

The selected-line identity gives

$$
A(x,P_L(x))=A(x,P_M(x))=0.
$$

The restriction $A(L(t),P_L(t))$ has degree at most $11919$ and at least $11920$ distinct roots. It is therefore identically zero. This holds for every labeled line graph of the first core.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_1$ be a first core, let $R$ be furnished by $P3$, and let $\mathcal A$ be the set of nonzero polynomials $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ of weighted degree at most $11919$ for weights $(1,1,87)$ such that $A_Z\ne0$ and $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every $L\in R$. Then $\mathcal A$ contains a squarefree polynomial $A$ satisfying $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every labeled line vertex $L$ of $G_1$.
lemmas.title: Squarefree Extension

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put

$$
h=\deg H,
\qquad
b=\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}B.
$$

Weighted leading forms multiply, and $H$ is independent of $Z$. Hence

$$
\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}A=h+b\le11919.
$$

Squarefreeness of $A$ implies squarefreeness of $B$, while $A_Z=HB_Z$ and $A_Z\ne0$ imply $B_Z\ne0$.

Suppose an irreducible polynomial $F$ divides both $B$ and $B_Z$. Write $B=FG$ with $F\nmid G$. Reducing

$$
B_Z=F_ZG+FG_Z
$$

modulo $F$ shows that $F\mid F_ZG$, and hence $F\mid F_Z$. Thus $F_Z=0$. Moreover,

$$
\deg_ZF\le\deg_ZB
\le\left\lfloor\frac{11919}{87}\right\rfloor
=137<147457.
$$

In characteristic $147457$, the equality $F_Z=0$ therefore forces $F$ to be independent of $Z$. Such an $F$ would divide every coefficient of $B$ as a polynomial in $Z$, contradicting the primitivity of $B$. Consequently,

$$
\gcd(B,B_Z)=1.
$$

Weighted differentiation with respect to $Z$ lowers weighted degree by $87$. Therefore

$$
\deg B\le b,
\qquad
\deg B_Z\le\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}B_Z\le b-87.
$$

Kominers–Thaler–Zheng Lemma $2.6$ bounds the number of labeled line graphs on which both $B$ and $B_Z$ vanish formally by $b(b-87)$. At most $h$ affine lines satisfy $H(L(t))\equiv0$. Writing $D=11919$, the total exceptional count is at most $h+b(b-87)$, and

$$
D(D-87)-\bigl(h+b(b-87)\bigr)
\ge(D-b)(D+b-88)\ge0.
$$

Thus the count is at most

$$
D(D-87)=11919\cdot11832=141025608.
$$

On a nonexceptional line, the identity $A(L(t),P_L(t))=H(L(t))B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ and the nonzero factor $H(L(t))$ imply $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$. Nonexceptionality makes $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ nonzero, and weighted substitution bounds its univariate degree by

$$
b-87\le11919-87=11832.
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $A$ be the squarefree polynomial furnished by $P5$. Regard $A$ as a polynomial in $Z$, let $H\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ be the greatest common divisor of its $Z$-coefficients, and write $A=HB$ with $B$ primitive in $Z$. Then among the first-core lines, at most $11919\cdot11832$ either satisfy $H(L(t))\equiv0$ or satisfy both $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ and $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$. For every other line $L$, the restriction $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ is nonzero and has degree at most $11832$.
lemmas.title: Primitive-Factor Cleanup

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $\Lambda=147457\cdot147458=21743714306$. The two first-core pruning losses from $P1$ have numerators $4663475082$ and $5653687178$ over $\Lambda$.

Delete the exceptional lines from $P6$. Their normalized loss is at most

$$
\frac{11919\cdot11832}{\Lambda}
=\frac{141025608}{\Lambda}.
$$

On every remaining line, $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $11832$. Delete every accepted incidence $(x,L)$ for which $B_Z(x,f(x))=0$. There are at most $11832$ such incidences per line, so the normalized loss is at most

$$
\frac{11832}{147457}
=\frac{1744723056}{\Lambda}.
$$

Next, alternately delete point vertices of current degree below $11920$ and line vertices of current degree below $10897$. The corresponding normalized losses are at most

$$
\frac{11919}{147458}
=\frac{1757539983}{\Lambda}
$$

and

$$
\frac{10896}{147457}
=\frac{1606702368}{\Lambda}.
$$

The six deletion numerators sum to

$$
C=4663475082+5653687178+141025608+1744723056
+1757539983+1606702368
=15567153275.
$$

The initial acceptance hypothesis exceeds this total charge because

$$
71593809\Lambda-10^8C
=1474331554>0.
$$

Thus some edge survives, and the final subgraph is nonempty. The last pruning stage gives minimum point degree $11920$ and minimum line degree $10897$. Every surviving incidence avoided the derivative-root deletion; since $B_Z(x,f(x))$ depends only on the point vertex and its table value, every retained point satisfies $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ be a point table, assign a univariate polynomial of degree at most $87$ to every affine line, and let the associated accepted incidence graph have normalized edge measure at least $71593809/10^8$. Let $B$ be the primitive factor obtained in $P6$. Then the accepted graph contains a nonempty subgraph of minimum point degree $11920$ and minimum line degree $10897$ such that every retained point $x$ satisfies $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.title: Simple-Root Core

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $p=147457$ and, for every affine line $L$, let $n_L=|X\cap L|$. Every point lies on $p+1$ affine lines, while every ordered pair of distinct points determines exactly one affine line. Consequently,

$$
\sum_L n_L=(p+1)|X|
$$

and

$$
\sum_L n_L^2=|X|^2+p|X|.
$$

Since the average of the $n_L$ is $|X|/p$, these identities give

$$
\sum_L\left(n_L-\frac{|X|}{p}\right)^2
=p^3a(1-a).
$$

Let $\mathbf 1_T(L)$ be the indicator of $T$. Centering both factors yields

$$
\sum_L\left(n_L-\frac{|X|}{p}\right)
\left(\mathbf 1_T(L)-b\right).
$$

The second centered square sum is

$$
\sum_L\left(\mathbf 1_T(L)-b\right)^2
=p(p+1)b(1-b).
$$

Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by division by the total incidence count $p^2(p+1)$, gives

$$
|J(X,T)-ab|
\le\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}}
=\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{147458}}.
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $X\subseteq\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ have density $a=|X|/147457^2$, and let $T$ be a set of affine lines with density $b=|T|/(147457\cdot147458)$. Define their normalized incidence measure by

$$
J(X,T)=\frac{|\{(x,L)\in X\times T:x\in L\}|}{147457^2\cdot147458}.
$$

Then

$$
|J(X,T)-ab|\le
\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{147458}}.
$$
lemmas.title: Centered Incidence Estimate

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $p=147457$. For a connected component, let $a$ be its point density, $b$ its line density, and $e$ its retained-edge count normalized by the total number of affine point-line incidences. Define

$$
\alpha=\frac{11920}{p+1},
\qquad
\beta=\frac{10897}{p},
\qquad
c=\frac{\alpha}{\beta},
\qquad
\gamma^2=\frac{1}{c(p+1)}
=\frac{10897}{11920p}.
$$

The minimum degrees from $P7$ give

$$
e\ge\alpha a,
\qquad
e\ge\beta b.
$$

The component edges are incidences between its point and line sets, so $P8$ gives

$$
e\le ab+
\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{p+1}}.
$$

If $a\ge\beta$, then $a>71593809/10^9$. Assume instead that $a<\beta$. If $\alpha a\ge\beta b$, then $b\le ca$ and $ca<\alpha<1/2$. The first lower bound and monotonicity of the upper bound in $b$ on this interval imply

$$
\beta\le a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.
$$

If $\beta b\ge\alpha a$, then $b\ge ca$. Dividing the second lower bound by $b$ and using $a/b\le1/c$ and $1-b\le1-ca$ gives the same inequality. Define

$$
\phi(a)=a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.
$$

The function $\phi$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\beta]$. Indeed, a sufficient uniform derivative inequality is

$$
4(1-\beta)(1-\alpha)>\gamma^2(1+c)^2.
$$

After clearing its positive denominators, the left-minus-right numerator is

$$
\begin{aligned}
&4\cdot11920\cdot10897\cdot147458
\cdot(147457-10897)\cdot(147458-11920)\\
&\quad-\bigl(10897\cdot147458+11920\cdot147457\bigr)^2\\
&=1418053613663866288195644>0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Set

$$
\tau=\frac{u}{v},
\qquad
u=71593809,
\qquad
v=10^9.
$$

The quantities needed for the endpoint comparison are positive because

$$
10897v-pu=339991706287>0
$$

and

$$
10897(p+1)v-11920pu
=1481010287138941040>0.
$$

Squaring the positive inequality $\beta-\tau>\gamma\sqrt{(1-\tau)(1-c\tau)}$ and clearing denominators gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
&11920(p+1)(10897v-pu)^2\\
&\quad-p(v-u)\bigl(10897(p+1)v-11920pu\bigr)\\
&=429837169915936597894692105360>0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $\phi(\tau)<\beta$. If $a\le\tau$, monotonicity would give

$$
\beta\le\phi(a)\le\phi(\tau)<\beta,
$$

a contradiction. Hence $a>\tau$. In particular,

$$
\tau p^2
=1556704771+\frac{966037841}{10^9},
$$

so every component has at least $1556704772$ point vertices.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $C$ be any connected component of the subgraph furnished by $P7$, and let $X_C$ be its set of point vertices. Then

$$
\frac{|X_C|}{147457^2}>\frac{71593809}{10^9}.
$$
lemmas.title: Component Density

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose a point vertex $x_0$ of the component. Its degree is at least

$$
11920>11919.
$$

Every incident retained line carries a label taking the common value $f(x_0)$ at $x_0$. The cleanup construction also gives

$$
B(x_0,f(x_0))=0,
\qquad
B_Z(x_0,f(x_0))\ne0,
\qquad
\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}B\le11919.
$$

After translating $x_0$ to the origin, Kominers–Thaler–Zheng Lemma $2.7$ constructs the unique coefficient-by-coefficient formal root through total order $87$. Let $Q$ be its total-degree-$87$ truncation. On every retained line through $x_0$, both $Q$ restricted to the line and the degree-at-most-$87$ label are truncations of the same simple formal root. They therefore coincide. These are also the fixed hypotheses of the seed-recovery statement in Kominers–Thaler–Zheng Lemma $6.1$.

For every monomial $X^iY^jZ^k$ of $B$, substituting a polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$ produces total degree at most $i+j+87k$. Hence

$$
\deg B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\le11919.
$$

This bivariate polynomial vanishes identically on at least $11920$ distinct retained lines through $x_0$. Kominers–Thaler–Zheng Lemma $2.5$ therefore gives

$$
B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0.
$$

Suppose propagation has reached a retained point $x$. Then $Q(x)=f(x)$ and $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$. On every adjacent retained line, the restrictions of $Q$ and the line label are polynomial roots of the same relation, share the value $f(x)$ at $x$, and have a simple root there. One-variable formal-root uniqueness makes the two restrictions equal. Consequently, $Q$ agrees with $f$ at every point joined to $x$ by such a line. Induction along paths in the connected component propagates the same $Q$ to every point vertex of the component.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For every connected component $C$ of the subgraph furnished by $P7$, there exists a polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that $Q(x)=f(x)$ for every point vertex $x$ of $C$.
lemmas.title: Componentwise Polynomial Recovery

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The subgraph from $P7$ is nonempty, so choose one of its connected components. By $P10$, a single polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$ agrees with $f$ at every point vertex of that component. By $P9$, the component has point density strictly greater than

$$
\frac{71593809}{10^9}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]
>\frac{71593809}{10^9},
$$

which implies the claimed weak inequality.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
In the fixed setting $m=2$, let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$, and assign a univariate polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$ to every affine line $L$. If a uniformly random affine line followed by a uniformly random point on that line satisfies $P_L(x)=f(x)$ with probability at least $71593809/10^8$, then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that

$$
\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]
\ge\frac{71593809}{10^9}.
$$
lemmas.title: Fixed-Instance Soundness

lemmas.proof_markdown:
There are

$$
147457^{\binom{89}{2}}=147457^{3916}
$$

bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$. Choose the values of $f$ independently and uniformly in $\mathbb F_{147457}$. For a fixed polynomial $Q$, let $X_Q$ be its number of agreements with $f$. The base-two exponential-moment bound gives

$$
\Pr[X_Q\ge2\cdot147457]
\le\frac{(1+1/147457)^{147457^2}}{4^{147457}}
<\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^{147457},
$$

where $e<49/18<11/4$ is used in the strict comparison. Since

$$
147457<2^{18},
\qquad
147457=2\cdot73728+1,
\qquad
\left(\frac{11}{16}\right)^2<\frac12,
$$

a union bound over all candidate polynomials is less than

$$
2^{18\cdot3916-73728}=2^{-3240}<1.
$$

Hence some deterministic table $f$ has fewer than $2\cdot147457$ agreements with every total-degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial, and thus agreement fraction below $2/147457$.

On every affine line, choose $88$ distinct points and interpolate the values of this $f$ by a univariate polynomial of degree at most $87$. Every line then has at least $88$ accepted points, so the test acceptance is at least $88/147457$. For every

$$
\varepsilon\in\left[\frac{20}{147457},\frac{88}{147457}\right],
$$

the acceptance is at least $\varepsilon$, while every degree-at-most-$87$ agreement is strictly below $2/147457\le\varepsilon/10$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
There exist a point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and degree-at-most-$87$ line labels whose test acceptance is at least $88/147457$ and such that every $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ satisfies

$$
\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]<\frac{2}{147457}.
$$

For every $\varepsilon\in[20/147457,88/147457]$, these tables refute the implication from acceptance at least $\varepsilon$ to degree-$87$ agreement at least $\varepsilon/10$.
lemmas.title: Low-Agreement Construction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Take $f(x)=0$ at every point. There are $147458$ affine-line directions. Choose exactly $105571$ of them, assign the zero polynomial to every line in those directions, and assign the constant polynomial $1$ to every other line. Every incidence on a zero-labeled line is accepted, and no incidence on a one-labeled line is accepted. Therefore

$$
\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)=\frac{105571}{147458}.
$$

The exact cross-product margin is

$$
105571\cdot10^8-71593809\cdot147458
=20112478>0,
$$

so this acceptance is greater than $71593809/10^8$. The constant polynomial $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ at every point and hence has agreement $1$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: There exist a point table on $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ and degree-at-most-$87$ line labels with test acceptance greater than $71593809/10^8$ such that all accepted lines occupy exactly $105571$ directions and a total-degree-zero polynomial agrees with the point table on every point.
lemmas.title: Directional Concentration

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The factorization

$$
B=(Z-X)(Z+X)
$$

has the two polynomial branches $Z=X$ and $Z=-X$. On $L_+(t)$, the label $t$ is the restriction of the first branch, while on $L_-(t)$, the label $-t$ is the restriction of the second. Both labels take the value $0$ at the common point $(0,0)$. Moreover,

$$
B_Z=2Z,
$$

so $B_Z(0,0,0)=0$. Thus the two incident lines can select different branches at their common labeled point.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let

$$
B(X,Y,Z)=Z^2-X^2\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z].
$$

The labeled lines

$$
L_+(t)=(t,0),\qquad P_{L_+}(t)=t
$$

and

$$
L_-(t)=(t,t),\qquad P_{L_-}(t)=-t
$$

satisfy $B(L_+(t),P_{L_+}(t))\equiv0$ and $B(L_-(t),P_{L_-}(t))\equiv0$, use different branches through the common labeled point $(0,0,0)$, and satisfy $B_Z(0,0,0)=0$.
lemmas.title: Singular Branching

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The table $f$ has $147457^2$ inputs and only $147457$ possible values. By the pigeonhole principle, some value $c\in\mathbb F_{147457}$ occurs at least $147457$ times. The constant polynomial $Q=c$ therefore has agreement at least

$$
\frac{147457}{147457^2}=\frac{1}{147457}.
$$

If $0<\varepsilon\le10/147457$, then

$$
\frac{\varepsilon}{10}\le\frac{1}{147457},
$$

so this constant polynomial has the required agreement.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For every point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and every $\varepsilon$ satisfying $0<\varepsilon\le10/147457$, there exists a total-degree-zero polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ such that

$$
\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]
\ge\frac{\varepsilon}{10}.
$$
lemmas.title: Constant-Polynomial Floor

lemmas.proof_markdown: Set $p=147457$. Charge each deleted point at most $31647$ incident edges and each deleted line at most $38484$ incident edges at its deletion. There are $p^2$ points and $p(p+1)$ affine lines, so the total charge is at most $31647p^2+38484p(p+1)=1524903761422407$. Every surviving vertex has degree strictly above its deletion threshold.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G$ be an accepted point-line incidence graph over $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. Iteratively delete point vertices of current degree at most $31647$ and line vertices of current degree at most $38484$. At most $1524903761422407$ edges are deleted. If the residual graph is nonempty, its point vertices have degree at least $31648$ and its line vertices have degree at least $38485$.
lemmas.title: First-core pruning

lemmas.proof_markdown: Set $p=147457$, $D=11915$, $\Lambda=p(p+1)$, and $\theta=2/158235$. Select each line vertex independently with probability $\theta$. Each accepted point on a fixed core line has at least $31647$ alternative covering lines. The alternative-line sets for distinct points of that line are disjoint, so the coverage indicators are independent. Since $\theta\cdot31647=2/5$, each point is covered with probability at least $1-e^{-2/5}>32967/100000$. For a core line containing $n\ge38485$ accepted points, Hoeffding's inequality bounds the probability of at most $D$ covered points by less than $e^{-31}$. Exact rational estimates give $\Lambda e^{-31}<751/10^6$, so every core line has more than $D$ covered points with probability greater than $999249/10^6$. Also $\mathbb E|R|\le2\Lambda/158235$. Markov's inequality and $275035\cdot158235\cdot999249-2\Lambda\cdot10^6=50970418025>0$ give $\Pr[|R|\ge275035]<999249/10^6$. The two strict failure bounds sum to less than $1$, so a simultaneous outcome exists with $|R|\le275034$ and more than $D$ covered points on every core line. The covering lines associated with distinct points of one fixed line are distinct, so $|R|>D$, equivalently $|R|\ge11916$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_0$ be a nonempty subgraph of the affine point-line incidence graph over $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ whose point vertices have degree at least $31648$ and whose line vertices have degree at least $38485$. There exists a subset $R$ of its line vertices with $11916\le |R|\le275034$ such that every line vertex $L$ has at least $11916$ distinct accepted point neighbors, each incident to a selected line in $R$ distinct from $L$.
lemmas.title: Sparse reaching family

lemmas.proof_markdown: Set $D=11915$. The space spanned by monomials $X^iY^jZ^k$ satisfying $i+j+87k\le D$ has dimension $\sum_{k=0}^{136}\binom{D-87k+2}{2}=3277308246$. Each selected line imposes at most $D+1=11916$ homogeneous linear conditions, while $275034\cdot11916=3277305144$, leaving a surplus of $3102$. Thus a nonzero interpolant exists. A nonzero $Z$-independent interpolant would have total degree at most $D$ and vanish on more than $D$ distinct affine lines, which is impossible. Hence the interpolant depends on $Z$. Its $Z$-degree is at most $136<147457$, so its $Z$-derivative is nonzero. Among the polynomials vanishing on the finite selected line-graph point set and having nonzero $Z$-derivative, choose one of minimum weighted degree. KTZ Lemma 2.3 makes this polynomial squarefree. Each restriction has degree at most $D<147457$ and vanishes at all $147457$ points of its selected line, so each restriction is the zero polynomial.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $R$ be a line set supplied by the sparse reaching construction, and for every $L\in R$ let $L(t)$ be an affine parametrization and $P_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ have degree at most $87$. There exists a squarefree polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that $\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)\le11915$, $A_Z\ne0$, and $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ in $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ for every $L\in R$.
lemmas.title: Weighted interpolant

lemmas.proof_markdown: Fix a line vertex $L$ of the first core and set $D=11915$. The sparse reaching property supplies more than $D$ accepted points of $L$ covered by selected lines. At each such point $x$, the two accepted line labels equal $f(x)$, and the selected-line identity gives $A(x,f(x))=0$. Hence $A(L(t),P_L(t))$ has more than $D$ distinct roots. Its degree is at most $D$, so it is identically zero.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_0$ be a first core, let $R$ satisfy the sparse reaching property in $G_0$, and let $A$ be the weighted interpolant for the selected degree-at-most-$87$ line labels. Then $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every line vertex $L$ of $G_0$.
lemmas.title: First-core identity extension

lemmas.proof_markdown: The highest weighted-homogeneous parts of $H$ and $B$ have a nonzero product, so $\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(A)=h+W\le11915$. Since $A_Z=HB_Z\ne0$, one has $n\ge1$ and $W\ge87n$. Thus $n\le\lfloor W/87\rfloor\le136<147457$. Ordinary degree is bounded by weighted degree, giving $\deg B\le W\le11915<147457$. Primitivity excludes every irreducible factor of $B$ that is independent of $Z$. Each remaining irreducible factor has positive $Z$-degree below $147457$ and therefore has nonzero $Z$-derivative. The squarefree polynomial $A$ has squarefree factor $B$, so reduction modulo each irreducible factor of $B$ shows that no such factor divides $B_Z$. Consequently $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ be the squarefree weighted interpolant whose identities extend to the first core. Write $A=HB$, where $H\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ is the coefficient content of $A$ as a polynomial in $Z$ and $B$ is primitive in $Z$. If $h=\deg H$, $W=\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)$, and $n=\deg_Z B$, then $h+W\le11915$, $1\le n\le136<147457$, $\deg B\le W\le11915<147457$, and $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$.
lemmas.title: Primitive separable factor

lemmas.proof_markdown: At most $h$ distinct affine lines satisfy $H(L(t))\equiv0$, since the defining form of every such line divides $H$. On every other line, the identity $H(L(t))B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ in the integral domain $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ gives $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$. Suppose first that $n\ge2$ and write $B=\sum_{i=0}^n b_iZ^i$. Since $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$, the discriminant $\Delta_Z(B)$ is nonzero. It has coefficient degree $2n-2$ and coefficient-index weight $n(n-1)$. Because $\deg b_i\le W-87i$, one obtains $\deg_{X,Y}\Delta_Z(B)\le(n-1)(2W-87n)$. If a non-content line is derivative-degenerate, then modulo its defining linear form, $P_L$ is a repeated finite root of $B$. Homogenization to nominal degree $n$ makes this a repeated projective root even when the specialized leading coefficient vanishes, so the line form divides $\Delta_Z(B)$. The number of content and derivative-degenerate lines is therefore at most $h+(n-1)(2W-87n)\le(n-1)(23830-87n)+(3-2n)h$. For $n\ge2$, the coefficient of $h$ is negative. For $F(n)=(n-1)(23830-87n)$, one has $F(n)-F(n-1)=2(11915-87(n-1))>0$ throughout $2\le n\le136$. The maximum is $135(23830-11832)=1619730$. If $n=1$, write $B=a_0+a_1Z$. A derivative-degenerate line divides $a_1$, and the identity $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ then makes it divide $a_0$, contradicting primitivity. Only content lines remain, and $h\le11915-87=11828$. Finally, on every nonexceptional line the derivative restriction is nonzero and has degree at most $W-87\le11828$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $\mathcal T$ be the family of first-core lines, with labels $P_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ of degree at most $87$. Let $A=HB$ satisfy the primitive-factor conclusions and suppose $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every $L\in\mathcal T$. Define $\mathcal E$ to contain every $L\in\mathcal T$ for which either $H(L(t))\equiv0$, or $H(L(t))\not\equiv0$ and $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$. Then $|\mathcal E|\le1619730$. For every $L\in\mathcal T\setminus\mathcal E$, one has $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, and $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ is nonzero of degree at most $11828$.
lemmas.title: Discriminant cleanup

lemmas.proof_markdown: Put $p=147457$, $\Lambda=p(p+1)=21743714306$, and $N=p^2(p+1)=3206262880419842$. Deleting all edges on exceptional lines and all remaining edges at derivative roots costs at most $1619730p+(\Lambda-1619730)11828=257404335171538$ edges. Alternately deleting points of current degree at most $11915$ and lines of current degree at most $10807$ costs at most $11915p^2+10807\Lambda=494058919510777$ further edges. Including the first-pruning loss, the total deletion budget is $M=1524903761422407+257404335171538+494058919510777=2276367016104722$. With $u=7099751645463$, the exact comparison $uN-10^{13}M=491243774476846>0$ shows that the acceptance hypothesis leaves a nonempty graph. Its construction gives minimum point degree $11916$ and minimum line degree $10808$. Every retained point is incident to a retained accepted line; the line identity and acceptance give $B(x,f(x))=0$, while the derivative-root deletion gives $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ be a point table, and for every affine line $L$ let $P_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ have degree at most $87$. Let $B$ be the primitive polynomial in the discriminant-cleanup construction. If the uniform affine-line-then-point acceptance probability is at least $7099751645463/10^{13}$, then the accepted incidence graph contains a nonempty subgraph $G_1$ of minimum point degree $11916$ and minimum line degree $10808$. Every retained line $L$ satisfies $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, and every retained point $x$ satisfies $B(x,f(x))=0$ and $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.title: Simple-root core

lemmas.proof_markdown: Put $p=147457$ and $n_L=|X\cap L|$. Every point lies on $p+1$ affine lines, and every ordered pair of distinct points determines one affine line. Hence $\sum_Ln_L=(p+1)|X|$ and $\sum_Ln_L^2=|X|^2+p|X|$. Since the mean of $n_L$ is $|X|/p$, these identities give $\sum_L(n_L-|X|/p)^2=p^3a(1-a)$. Also $\sum_L(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal T}(L)-b)^2=p(p+1)b(1-b)$. Centering both factors gives $p^2(p+1)(J(X,\mathcal T)-ab)=\sum_L(n_L-|X|/p)(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal T}(L)-b)$. Cauchy--Schwarz and division by $p^2(p+1)$ yield the stated inequality.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ and let $\mathcal T$ be a set of affine lines. Define $a=|X|/147457^2$, $b=|\mathcal T|/(147457\cdot147458)$, and $J(X,\mathcal T)=|\{(x,L)\in X\times\mathcal T:x\in L\}|/(147457^2\cdot147458)$. Then $|J(X,\mathcal T)-ab|\le\sqrt{a(1-a)b(1-b)/147458}$.
lemmas.title: Centered incidence bound

lemmas.proof_markdown: Put $p=147457$. Let $a$ and $b$ be the point and line densities of a connected component, and let $e$ be its edge count divided by $p^2(p+1)$. Define $\alpha=11916/(p+1)$, $\beta=10808/p$, $c=\alpha/\beta=11916p/(10808(p+1))$, and $\gamma^2=1/(c(p+1))=10808/(11916p)$. The minimum degrees and the centered incidence bound give $e\ge\alpha a$, $e\ge\beta b$, and $e\le U_a(b):=ab+\sqrt{a(1-a)b(1-b)/(p+1)}$. Set $b_0=ca$, so $\alpha a=\beta b_0$. Whenever $a<\beta$ and $b_0<1/2$, feasibility implies $F(a):=(\beta-a)^2-\gamma^2(1-a)(1-ca)\le0$. Indeed, if $F(a)>0$, then $U_a(b_0)<\alpha a$. For $b\le b_0$, the function $U_a(b)$ is increasing, contradicting $e\ge\alpha a$; for $b\ge b_0$, the function $U_a(b)/b$ is decreasing, contradicting $e\ge\beta b$. Let $u=7099751645463$, $T_0=10^{14}$, $\tau=u/T_0$, and $A_0=10808T_0-up=33891921614962409$. Thus $\tau<\beta$. The inequality $c\tau<1/2$ follows from $10808(p+1)T_0-2\cdot11916pu=134422693075927784131288>0$. After clearing the positive denominator of $F(\tau)$, its numerator is $11916(p+1)A_0^2+11916p^2u(T_0-u)-10808p(p+1)T_0(T_0-u)=6005223431415950878446170373383442224972>0$. The estimates $\beta-\tau>1/500$, $c<9/8$, and $\gamma^2<1/160000$ are certified respectively by $500A_0-pT_0=2200260807481204500>0$, $9\cdot10808(p+1)-8\cdot11916p=286753680>0$, and $11916p-160000\cdot10808=27817612>0$. For $0\le a\le\tau$, one has $F'(a)=2(a-\beta)+\gamma^2(1+c-2ca)<-1/250+17/1280000=-5103/1280000<0$. Hence $F(a)\ge F(\tau)>0$ throughout $[0,\tau]$, contradicting feasibility. Therefore $a>\tau$. Finally, $up^2=1543739245T_0+14422488056087$, so the component's integer point count is at least $1543739246$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_1$ be a graph supplied by the simple-root-core construction, let $C$ be a connected component of $G_1$, and let $X_C$ be its point-vertex set. Then $|X_C|/147457^2>7099751645463/10^{14}$ and $|X_C|\ge1543739246$.
lemmas.title: Component point mass

lemmas.proof_markdown: Choose a point $x$ in the component and put $D=11915$. It lies on at least $11916>D$ retained lines. On this star, $\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)\le D$, every line label has degree at most $87$, all labels have common value $f(x)$, every line identity holds, and $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$. KTZ Lemmas 2.7 and 6.1 produce $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ satisfying $B(X,Y,Q)=0$ and agreeing with the seed-star labels. At any reached accepted point, $Q$ and the next line label solve the same univariate equation and share a simple value. Formal simple-root uniqueness makes their restrictions identical. KTZ Lemma 6.3 propagates this equality along every path in the connected component, so $Q=f$ at every point vertex of the component.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For every connected component $C$ of a graph supplied by the simple-root-core construction, there exists a polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that $Q(x)=f(x)$ for every point vertex $x$ of $C$.
lemmas.title: Componentwise polynomial recovery

lemmas.proof_markdown: The simple-root-core lemma supplies a nonempty component. The componentwise recovery lemma supplies a polynomial $Q$ on it, and the component-mass lemma gives agreement strictly above $7099751645463/10^{14}$. The claimed acceptance threshold is below the configured comparison value $1$ and below the prior unaudited value $0.717920394295$, since $0.7179203942950-0.7099751645463=79452297487/10^{13}=0.0079452297487>0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ be a point table. For every affine line $L$, let $L(t)$ be an affine parametrization and let $P_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ have degree at most $87$. If $L$ is uniform among affine lines and $t$ is uniform in $\mathbb F_{147457}$, and $\Pr_{L,t}[P_L(t)=f(L(t))]\ge7099751645463/10^{13}$, then there exists $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that $\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]>7099751645463/10^{14}$.
lemmas.title: Fixed-instance soundness

lemmas.proof_markdown: The coefficients of $B$ as a polynomial in $Z$ include $1$ and $-X$, so their greatest common divisor is $1$. Moreover, $\partial B/\partial X=-1$. Any repeated irreducible factor of $B$ would divide every formal partial derivative, contradicting this identity; hence $B$ is squarefree. Finally, $B_Z=147457Z^{147456}=0$ in characteristic $147457$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $B(X,Y,Z)=Z^{147457}-X\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$. Then $B$ is primitive as a polynomial in $Z$, is squarefree in $\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$, and satisfies $B_Z=0$.
lemmas.title: Frobenius derivative example

lemmas.proof_markdown: The polynomial $A$ has the factor $X$, while the first coordinate of $L(t)$ is identically zero. Therefore $A(0,t,P(t))=0\cdot(P(t)-t)\equiv0$ for every polynomial $P(t)$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $A(X,Y,Z)=X(Z-Y)\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ and let $L(t)=(0,t)$ parametrize the affine line $X=0$. For every $P\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$, one has $A(0,t,P(t))\equiv0$.
lemmas.title: Coefficient-content example

lemmas.proof_markdown: One has $B_Z=2Z$, so both restrictions vanish for the zero label. The discriminant of $Z^2-X$ is $0^2-4(1)(-X)=4X$. Since $4\ne0$ in $\mathbb F_{147457}$, the factor $X$ occurs with multiplicity exactly $1$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $B(X,Y,Z)=Z^2-X$, let $L(t)=(0,t)$ parametrize the line $X=0$, and let $P_L(t)=0$. Then $B(0,t,P_L(t))\equiv0$, $B_Z(0,t,P_L(t))\equiv0$, and $\operatorname{disc}_Z(B)=4X$. The defining form $X$ of $L$ divides $\operatorname{disc}_Z(B)$ with multiplicity exactly $1$.
lemmas.title: Discriminant multiplicity example

lemmas.proof_markdown: Because $147457>11828$, choose distinct $a_1,\ldots,a_{11828}\in\mathbb F_{147457}$. The factors $Z$ and $Z+g(X)$ are distinct and coprime, so $B$ is squarefree; its leading $Z$-coefficient is $1$, so it is primitive. For weights $(1,1,87)$, the terms have weights $174$ and $87+11828=11915$, giving $\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)=11915$. Moreover, $B_Z=2Z+g(X)$, so on the zero-labeled line $L(t)=(t,0)$ its restriction is $g(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{11828}(t-a_i)$, which is nonzero and has exactly $11828$ roots.
lemmas.statement_markdown: There exist distinct elements $a_1,\ldots,a_{11828}\in\mathbb F_{147457}$. Define $g(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{11828}(X-a_i)$ and $B(X,Y,Z)=Z(Z+g(X))$, let $L(t)=(t,0)$, and let $P_L(t)=0$. Then $B$ is primitive and squarefree, has $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree exactly $11915$, satisfies $B(t,0,P_L(t))\equiv0$, and has a nonzero derivative restriction $B_Z(t,0,P_L(t))=g(t)$ with exactly $11828$ roots in $\mathbb F_{147457}$.
lemmas.title: Derivative-root example

lemmas.proof_markdown: There are $147458$ distinct lines through the origin, so one may choose $11915$ pairwise nonproportional homogeneous linear forms $\ell_i$. Their product has total degree $11915$. Since $Z$ has weight $87$, one has $\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)=11915$, and direct differentiation gives $B_Z=1$. On $L_i$, the factor $\ell_i$ vanishes identically, so the zero label satisfies the required identity. If $Q$ were a global polynomial root, then $0=B(X,Y,Q)=Q-\prod_{i=1}^{11915}\ell_i$, forcing $Q=\prod_{i=1}^{11915}\ell_i$, whose total degree is $11915>87$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: There exist $11915$ pairwise nonproportional homogeneous linear forms $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_{11915}\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$. Let $L_i$ be the line $\ell_i=0$, assign the constant label $P_{L_i}(t)=0$, and define $B(X,Y,Z)=Z-\prod_{i=1}^{11915}\ell_i(X,Y)$. Then all $L_i$ pass through one point, $\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}(B)=11915$, $B_Z=1$, and $B(L_i(t),P_{L_i}(t))\equiv0$ for $1\le i\le11915$. There is no $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ satisfying $B(X,Y,Q)\equiv0$.
lemmas.title: Seed-star example

lemmas.proof_markdown: The factorization $B=(Z-X)(Z+X)$ gives the two polynomial branches $Z=X$ and $Z=-X$. Both labels equal $0$ at the common point, where $B_Z=2Z$ vanishes. If $B(X,Y,Q)=0$, then the integral-domain identity $(Q-X)(Q+X)=0$ forces $Q=X$ or $Q=-X$. The first choice does not restrict to $-t$ on $L_-$, while the second does not restrict to $t$ on $L_+$. Thus the mixed linewise roots cannot be propagated to one global polynomial root when pointwise simplicity is absent.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $B(X,Y,Z)=Z^2-X^2$, $L_+(t)=(t,0)$ with $P_{L_+}(t)=t$, and $L_-(t)=(t,t)$ with $P_{L_-}(t)=-t$. Both labels have degree at most $87$. They satisfy $B(L_+(t),P_{L_+}(t))\equiv0$ and $B(L_-(t),P_{L_-}(t))\equiv0$, take the common value $0$ at $(0,0)$, and obey $B_Z(0,0,0)=0$. There is no $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ satisfying $B(X,Y,Q)\equiv0$ whose restrictions to $L_+$ and $L_-$ are respectively $P_{L_+}$ and $P_{L_-}$.
lemmas.title: Branch-switching example

lemmas.proof_markdown: Every line whose direction lies in $\mathcal D$ carries the zero label and accepts all $147457$ points. Every remaining line carries the label $1$ and accepts no point because $f$ is identically zero. Every direction contains the same number of affine lines, so the acceptance is $104692/147458$. The exact comparison is $104692\cdot10^{13}-7099751645463\cdot147458=4821863316946>0$. Finally, $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ everywhere.
lemmas.statement_markdown: There exist a set $\mathcal D$ of exactly $104692$ affine-line directions in $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$, a point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ with $f(x)=0$, and constant labels $P_L=0$ when $\operatorname{dir}(L)\in\mathcal D$ and $P_L=1$ otherwise. Their acceptance probability is $104692/147458>7099751645463/10^{13}$, their accepted lines are supported on exactly the directions in $\mathcal D$, and the total-degree-$0$ polynomial $Q=0$ agrees with $f$ everywhere.
lemmas.title: Directional concentration example

lemmas.proof_markdown: Put $p=147457$. The vector space of bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $87$ has dimension $\binom{89}{2}=3916$, so it contains $p^{3916}$ polynomials. For uniformly random $f$, the agreement count with any fixed polynomial is distributed as $\operatorname{Bin}(p^2,1/p)$ and has mean $p$. A Chernoff bound gives $\Pr[|\{x:Q(x)=f(x)\}|\ge2p]\le(e/4)^p<(11/16)^p$. The inequalities $p<2^{18}$, $(11/16)^2<1/2$, and $p>2(18\cdot3916+3240)$ imply $p^{3916}(11/16)^p<2^{-3240}<1$. A union bound therefore supplies a deterministic $f$ with fewer than $2p$ agreements with every total-degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial. On each affine line, interpolate the values of $f$ at any $88$ distinct points. The resulting line label has degree at most $87$ and accepts at least $88$ points, so the overall acceptance is at least $88/p$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: There exist a point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and, for every affine line $L$, a label $P_L\in\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ of degree at most $87$ such that the uniform affine-line-then-point acceptance probability is at least $88/147457$, while every $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ satisfies $|\{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2:Q(x)=f(x)\}|/147457^2<2/147457$.
lemmas.title: Low-agreement construction

lemmas.proof_markdown: The table has $147457^2$ inputs and only $147457$ possible values. By the pigeonhole principle, some $c\in\mathbb F_{147457}$ occurs at least $147457$ times. The constant polynomial $Q(X,Y)=c$ therefore has agreement at least $147457/147457^2=1/147457$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For every point table $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$, there exists a constant polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ such that $|\{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2:Q(x)=f(x)\}|/147457^2\ge1/147457$.
lemmas.title: Constant agreement floor

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The primality certificate uses

$$147457-1=2^{14}\cdot 3^2.$$

Repeated squaring gives

$$10^{147456}\equiv 1,\qquad 10^{73728}\equiv 147456,\qquad 10^{49152}\equiv 78348\pmod{147457}.$$

Moreover,

$$\gcd(147455,147457)=\gcd(78347,147457)=1.$$

These congruences verify the required Pocklington conditions for the prime divisors $2$ and $3$ of $147456$, so $147457$ is prime.

An affine plane over a field of order $p$ has $p^2$ points and $p(p+1)$ affine lines. Every line contains $p$ points, so the number of line-point incidences is $p^2(p+1)$. At $p=147457$, these quantities are

$$p^2=21743566849,$$

$$p(p+1)=21743714306,$$

and

$$p^2(p+1)=3206262880419842.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p=147457$. Then $p$ is prime, and the affine plane $\mathbb F_p^2$ has $21743566849$ points, $21743714306$ affine lines, and $3206262880419842$ line-point incidences.
lemmas.title: Affine-plane data

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put

$$p=147457,\qquad n=p+1=147458,\qquad \Lambda=p(p+1)=21743714306,$$

and let $k_x$ be the accepted degree of a point $x$. Then

$$\sum_x k_x=AN,\qquad \frac{1}{p^2}\sum_x k_x=nA.$$

Choose uniformly an $r$-element subset $\mathcal R$ of all affine lines, where $r=362504$. For an accepted edge $(x,L)$, there are exactly $s=k_x-1$ eligible alternative accepted lines through $x$. Its exact no-hit probability is

$$\frac{\binom{\Lambda-s}{r}}{\binom{\Lambda}{r}}.$$

Writing $u=s/\Lambda$, sampling without replacement gives

$$\frac{\binom{\Lambda-s}{r}}{\binom{\Lambda}{r}}\le (1-u)^r.$$

Also,

$$(1-u)^{-r}=\left(1+\frac{u}{1-u}\right)^r\ge 1+\frac{ru}{1-u},$$

and hence

$$1-(1-u)^r\ge \frac{ru}{1+(r-1)u}.$$

Thus the coverage probability of $(x,L)$ is at least

$$\frac{r(k_x-1)}{\Lambda+(r-1)(k_x-1)}.$$

Define

$$H(t)=\frac{rt(t-1)}{\Lambda+(r-1)(t-1)}.$$

For $\lambda=\Lambda/(r-1)>1$,

$$H''(t)=\frac{2r\lambda(\lambda-1)}{(r-1)(\lambda+t-1)^3}>0.$$

Therefore $H$ is convex. Jensen's inequality over the $p^2$ points gives

$$\frac{\mathbb E_{\mathcal R}|C_{\mathcal R}|}{N}\ge \Phi(A),$$

where

$$\Phi(A)=\frac{rA(nA-1)}{\Lambda+(r-1)(nA-1)}.$$

The function $\Phi$ is increasing whenever $nA\ge 1$. Since

$$A\ge \frac{11518201}{20000000},$$

averaging over the choices of $\mathcal R$ supplies a deterministic family of exactly $362504$ lines satisfying

$$\frac{|C_{\mathcal R}|}{N}\ge \Phi\left(\frac{11518201}{20000000}\right)=\frac{443226125540836902604977}{1313200720651467717500000}.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$, and for every affine line $L$ let $P_L$ be a univariate polynomial over $\mathbb F_{147457}$ of degree at most $87$. Let $E$ be the set of incidences $(x,L)$ such that $P_L(x)=f(x)$, put $N=3206262880419842$, and set $A=|E|/N$. If

$$A\ge \frac{11518201}{20000000},$$

then there exists a set $\mathcal R$ of exactly $362504$ affine lines such that, for

$$C_{\mathcal R}=\{(x,L)\in E:\text{ there exists }M\in\mathcal R\text{ with }M\ne L\text{ and }(x,M)\in E\},$$

one has

$$\frac{|C_{\mathcal R}|}{N}\ge \frac{443226125540836902604977}{1313200720651467717500000}.$$
lemmas.title: Exact pencil coverage

lemmas.proof_markdown:
