For $D=13689$, the number of monomials of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $D$ is

$$\sum_{j=0}^{157}\binom{13689-87j+2}{2}=4962679907.$$

For each selected labeled-line graph, the identity

$$A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv 0$$

imposes at most $D+1=13690$ homogeneous linear constraints on the coefficients of $A$. The total number of constraints is at most

$$362504\cdot 13690=4962679760<4962679907.$$

Consequently, a nonzero interpolant exists.

If this interpolant were independent of $Z$, it would be a bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $D$ vanishing formally on $362504>D$ distinct affine lines. This contradicts KTZ revision $1$, Lemma $2.5$. Hence the interpolant depends on $Z$. Its $Z$-degree satisfies

$$\deg_Z A\le \left\lfloor\frac{13689}{87}\right\rfloor=157<147457,$$

so its $Z$-derivative is nonzero.

Factor the interpolant into irreducible factors and replace it by the product of its distinct irreducible factors. On each selected graph, the original product specializes to zero in the domain $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$, so at least one irreducible factor specializes to zero there. The product of all distinct factors therefore also specializes to zero on that graph. This replacement preserves $Z$-dependence, does not increase weighted degree, and makes the interpolant squarefree. Renaming the resulting polynomial as $A$ proves the claim.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $\mathcal R$ be a selected family supplied by P2, and let $\{P_L:L\in\mathcal R\}$ be its degree-at-most-$87$ line table. Then there exists a nonzero squarefree polynomial

$$A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$$

of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $13689$ such that $A_Z\ne 0$ and

$$A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv 0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$$

for every $L\in\mathcal R$.
lemmas.title: Squarefree weighted interpolation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For every affine line $L$, let $c_L$ be the number of edges of $C_{\mathcal R}$ incident to $L$. At each such edge $(x,L)$, there is a selected alternative accepted line $M$ through $x$. The selected-line identity gives

$$A(x,P_M(x))=0.$$

Both incidences are accepted, so

$$P_M(x)=f(x)=P_L(x),$$

and consequently

$$A(x,P_L(x))=0.$$

The restriction $A(L(t),P_L(t))$ has degree at most $D=13689$. If $c_L>D$, it has more than $D$ distinct roots and therefore vanishes identically. Lines with $c_L\le D$ account for at most $D$ covered edges each. Since there are $21743714306$ affine lines, at most

$$13689\cdot21743714306$$

covered edges lie on lines below the identity threshold. Retaining all accepted edges on the remaining identity lines yields the stated bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Under the hypotheses and notation of P2 and P3, let

$$\mathcal I_A=\{L:A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv 0\}.$$

Then

$$|\{(x,L)\in E:L\in\mathcal I_A\}|\ge |C_{\mathcal R}|-13689\cdot21743714306.$$
lemmas.title: Identity-line transfer

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Write

$$A=HB,$$

where $H\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ is the greatest common divisor of the coefficients of $A$ as a polynomial in $Z$, and $B$ is primitive in $Z$. Put

$$h=\deg H,\qquad W=\operatorname{wdeg}(B),\qquad z=\deg_Z B.$$

Weighted leading forms give

$$h+W=\operatorname{wdeg}(A)\le D=13689.$$

The polynomial $B$ is squarefree. Primitivity excludes every $Z$-independent irreducible factor of $B$. Since

$$z\le157<147457,$$

each irreducible factor has nonzero $Z$-derivative. It follows that

$$\gcd(B,B_Z)=1.$$

Hence the nominal-degree discriminant

$$\Delta=\operatorname{Disc}^{(z)}_Z(B)$$

is nonzero. If

$$B=\sum_i b_iZ^i,$$

then

$$\deg b_i\le W-87i.$$

Every discriminant monomial has coefficient degree $2z-2$ and coefficient-index weight $z(z-1)$, so

$$\deg\Delta\le(z-1)(2W-87z).$$

At most $h$ identity lines satisfy $H(L(t))\equiv0$. On any other formal $A$-identity line, the domain property of $\mathbb F_{147457}[t]$ gives

$$B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0.$$

If also

$$B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0,$$

then over $\mathbb F_{147457}(t)$ the nominal-degree homogenization of the specialized polynomial has the singular finite root $[P_L(t):1]$. Euler's identity applies because

$$1\le z\le157<147457.$$

Thus the specialized nominal-degree discriminant is zero even when the leading $Z$-coefficient drops, and the defining linear form of $L$ divides $\Delta$.

For $z\ge2$, the total number of content and derivative-degenerate identity lines is at most

$$h+(z-1)(2W-87z)\le(z-1)(2D-87z).$$

As $z$ increases through $2,\ldots,157$, the relevant successive increment is

$$2(D-87(z-1))>0.$$

The maximum is therefore

$$(157-1)(2\cdot13689-87\cdot157)=156(27378-13659)=2140164.$$

For $z=1$, a derivative-degenerate noncontent identity line would divide both coefficients of $B$, contrary to primitivity. The content count in this case is at most

$$D-87<2140164.$$

Thus there are at most

$$E_0=2140164$$

exceptional lines. On every nonexceptional identity line, the nonzero restriction $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ has degree at most

$$W-87\le D-87=13602=R_0.$$

Delete every accepted incidence on an exceptional line and every derivative-zero accepted incidence on a nonexceptional identity line. If the actual exceptional-line count is $e\le E_0$, the number deleted is at most

$$ep+(\Lambda-e)R_0.$$

This expression is increasing in $e$ because $p>R_0$. Hence the deletion count is at most

$$E_0p+(\Lambda-E_0)R_0=296044473642432.$$

Every remaining line has a formal $B$-identity. At every remaining accepted edge $(x,L)$, acceptance and that identity give $B(x,f(x))=0$, while the derivative-zero deletion gives $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $A$ and its formal identity lines be as in P3 and P4. Then there are polynomials

$$H\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y],\qquad B\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$$

such that $A=HB$ and $B$ is primitive in $Z$, and one can delete at most $296044473642432$ accepted incidences supported on the formal $A$-identity lines so that every surviving line $L$ satisfies

$$B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0,$$

and every surviving edge $(x,L)$ satisfies

$$B(x,f(x))=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0.$$
lemmas.title: Primitive discriminant cleanup

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The acceptance hypothesis exceeds

$$\epsilon_0=\frac{11518201}{20000000},$$

so P2 supplies covered-edge density at least

$$\frac{443226125540836902604977}{1313200720651467717500000}.$$

After the identity-line and discriminant cleanup, repeatedly delete any point of current degree at most $13689$ and any line of current degree at most $8776$. The process is iterative, and each vertex is charged only when it is deleted. The point-deletion charge is therefore at most

$$13689\cdot147457^2=297647686595961,$$

and the line-deletion charge is at most

$$8776\cdot21743714306=190822836749456.$$

Together with the identity-extension charge and the algebraic cleanup charge, the complete deletion charge is

$$13689\cdot21743714306+296044473642432+13689\cdot147457^2+8776\cdot21743714306$$

$$=297649705134834+296044473642432+297647686595961+190822836749456$$

$$=1082164702122683.$$

The exact comparison with the coverage lower bound is

$$443226125540836902604977\cdot3206262880419842$$

$$\quad-1082164702122683\cdot1313200720651467717500000$$

$$=7262802015573137406231186253634>0.$$

Thus the deletion process cannot remove every edge. In the remaining nonempty graph, no point has degree at most $13689$ and no line has degree at most $8776$. Its minimum point and line degrees are therefore at least $13690$ and $8777$, respectively, and all formal $B$-identities and simple-root conditions survive from P5.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and let $\{P_L\}$ be a family of affine-line polynomials of degree at most $87$. If

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{16}},$$

then the accepted-incidence graph has a nonempty retained subgraph of minimum point degree at least $13690$ and minimum line degree at least $8777$. There is a primitive polynomial $B\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ such that every retained line $L$ satisfies

$$B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0,$$

and every retained edge $(x,L)$ satisfies

$$B(x,f(x))=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0.$$
lemmas.title: Two-sided peeling

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For each affine line $L$, put

$$m_L=|X\cap L|.$$

Counting point-line incidences gives

$$\sum_Lm_L=(p+1)|X|.$$

Counting ordered pairs of points of $X$ lying on a common line gives

$$\sum_Lm_L^2=|X|^2+p|X|.$$

Indeed, each diagonal ordered pair lies on $p+1$ lines, while each ordered pair of distinct points determines one line. Consequently,

$$\frac1\Lambda\sum_L\left(\frac{m_L}{p}-a\right)^2=\frac{a(1-a)}{p+1},$$

where $p=147457$ and $\Lambda=p(p+1)$. Centering the indicator of $T$ gives

$$I(X,T)-ab=\frac1\Lambda\sum_L\bigl(\mathbf 1_T(L)-b\bigr)\left(\frac{m_L}{p}-a\right).$$

The mean square of the first centered factor is $b(1-b)$, and the mean square of the second is $a(1-a)/(p+1)$. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore yields

$$|I(X,T)-ab|\le\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{147458}}.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $X\subseteq\mathbb F_{147457}^2$ and let $T$ be a set of affine lines. Define

$$a=\frac{|X|}{147457^2},\qquad b=\frac{|T|}{21743714306},$$

and let

$$I(X,T)=\frac{|\{(x,L):x\in X,\ L\in T,\ x\in L\}|}{3206262880419842}.$$

Then

$$|I(X,T)-ab|\le\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{147458}}.$$
lemmas.title: Centered incidence mixing

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For a connected component, let $a$ be its point density, $b$ its line density, and $e$ its retained-edge density normalized by

$$N=3206262880419842.$$

Set

$$\alpha=\frac{13690}{147458}=\frac{6845}{73729},\qquad \beta=\frac{8777}{147457},$$

$$c=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}=\frac{1009343165}{647119433},\qquad \gamma^2=\frac1{c\cdot147458}=\frac{8777}{2018686330}.$$

The two minimum-degree bounds give

$$e\ge\alpha a,\qquad e\ge\beta b.$$

The centered incidence bound gives

$$e\le U_a(b):=ab+\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{147458}}.$$

Suppose $a<\beta$ and put

$$b_0=ca,$$

so that $\alpha a=\beta b_0$. Since $c\beta=\alpha<1/2$, one has $b_0<1/2$. Define

$$F(a)=(\beta-a)^2-\gamma^2(1-a)(1-ca)$$

and

$$\phi(a)=a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.$$

If $F(a)>0$, then $\phi(a)<\beta$ and

$$U_a(b_0)=ca\,\phi(a)<ca\beta=\alpha a.$$

For $b\le b_0$, the function $U_a(b)$ is increasing, contradicting $e\ge\alpha a$. For $b\ge b_0$, the function $U_a(b)/b$ is decreasing, contradicting $e\ge\beta b$. Hence every feasible component with $a<\beta$ satisfies

$$F(a)\le0,$$

and therefore

$$\beta\le\phi(a).$$

Let

$$\tau=\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{17}}.$$

Exactly,

$$\beta-\tau=\frac{28480317571499852543}{14745700000000000000000}>0.$$

The following rational comparisons hold:

$$c<\frac85,$$

because

$$8\cdot647119433-5\cdot1009343165=130239639>0;$$

$$\beta<\frac1{16},$$

because

$$147457-16\cdot8777=7025>0;$$

and

$$\gamma<\frac1{400},$$

because

$$2018686330-160000\cdot8777=614366330>0.$$

For $0\le z\le\beta$, these inequalities imply

$$\sqrt{(1-z)(1-cz)}>\frac9{10}$$

and

$$\phi'(z)=1-\frac{\gamma(1+c-2cz)}{2\sqrt{(1-z)(1-cz)}}>1-\frac{13}{3600}>0.$$

Finally,

$$F(\tau)=\frac{44654755643204526648386602209580933351747417}{43893738832947636980000000000000000000000000000000000}>0.$$

Since $\beta-\tau>0$, this gives $\phi(\tau)<\beta$. The monotonicity of $\phi$ rules out $a\le\tau$ when $a<\beta$, while $a\ge\beta$ already implies $a>\tau$. Thus every component has $a>\tau$.

Moreover,

$$\tau\,147457^2=\frac{125223386711859346243566849}{10^{17}},$$

so the strict density inequality implies that every component contains at least $1252233868$ points.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $G_*$ be a retained graph supplied by P6, and let $K$ be any connected component of $G_*$. If $X_K$ is the point-vertex set of $K$, then

$$\frac{|X_K|}{147457^2}>\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{17}}.$$
lemmas.title: Component mass

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose a point $b$ in the component and translate $b$ to the origin. The retained-edge conditions give

$$B(b,f(b))=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_Z(b,f(b))\ne0.$$

KTZ revision $1$, Lemma $2.7$, applied with $k=87$, gives a unique polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$, with $Q(b)=f(b)$, such that

$$B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0\pmod{\mathfrak m_b^{88}}.$$

At least $13690=D+1$ retained lines pass through $b$. On each such line $L$, the restrictions of $Q$ and $P_L$ are degree-at-most-$87$ formal roots with the same constant term. The one-variable specialization of Lemma $2.7$ therefore gives

$$Q|_L=P_L.$$

Substituting a polynomial of total degree at most $87$ into a relation of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $D=13689$ shows that

$$\deg_{\mathrm{tot}}B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\le D.$$

This polynomial vanishes formally on more than $D$ distinct lines through $b$. KTZ revision $1$, Lemma $2.5$, therefore gives

$$B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))\equiv0.$$

Suppose a retained line $L$ has already been reached and satisfies $Q|_L=P_L$. At every retained edge $(x,L)$,

$$Q(x)=P_L(x)=f(x)$$

and

$$B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0.$$

For every next retained line $M$ adjacent at $x$, both $Q|_M$ and $P_M$ are degree-at-most-$87$ roots of the same one-variable relation and have the same value $f(x)$ at the simple root. One-variable simple-root uniqueness gives

$$Q|_M=P_M.$$

Connectivity propagates the same fixed polynomial $Q$ through the entire component, and every component point lies on a retained edge. Hence $Q(x)=f(x)$ at every point of the component.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $K$ be any connected component of a retained graph supplied by P6, and let $X_K$ be its point-vertex set. Then there exists

$$Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$$

of total degree at most $87$ such that

$$Q(x)=f(x)$$

for every $x\in X_K$.
lemmas.title: Simple-root propagation

lemmas.proof_markdown:
By P6, the accepted-incidence graph has a nonempty retained component. By P8, every such component has point density strictly greater than

$$\tau=\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{17}}.$$

By P9, one polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$ agrees with $f$ at every point of that component. Therefore its global agreement probability is greater than $\tau$, and in particular is at least $\tau$.

The padding between the displayed acceptance threshold and the survival threshold is

$$\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{16}}-\frac{11518201}{20000000}=10^{-16}.$$

If the displayed JSON score is parsed as an IEEE-754 binary64 number, its exact value is

$$\frac{648417071644731}{1125899906842624}.$$

This value exceeds the survival threshold by

$$\frac{5471}{87960930222080000000}$$

and is below the exact displayed decimal by

$$\frac{6494322309}{171798691840000000000000000}.$$

Thus the weaker survival input remains valid, while P8 supplies the larger exact displayed agreement target. Finally,

$$\frac{7099751645463}{10^{13}}-\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{16}}=\frac{1340651145462999}{10^{16}}>0,$$

which proves the strict score comparison.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For every function

$$f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$$

and every family $\{P_L\}$ of affine-line polynomials of degree at most $87$, if

$$\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{16}},$$

then there exists a polynomial

$$Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$$

of total degree at most $87$ such that

$$\Pr_{x\in\mathbb F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]\ge\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{17}}.$$

Moreover,

$$\frac{5759100500000001}{10^{16}}<\frac{7099751645463}{10^{13}}.$$
lemmas.title: Soundness threshold

lemmas.proof_markdown:
There are $p+1=147458$ directions and $p=147457$ affine lines in each direction. Hence the number of affine lines is $\Lambda=p(p+1)=21743714306$, and multiplying by the $p$ points on each line gives $N=p\Lambda=p^2(p+1)=3206262880419842$ incidences.

A monomial $X^iY^jZ^z$ has weight $i+j+87z$. Thus $0\le z\le\lfloor17642/87\rfloor=202$, and for fixed $z$ there are $\binom{17642-87z+2}{2}$ choices of $(i,j)$. Therefore
$$V_D=\sum_{z=0}^{202}\binom{17642-87z+2}{2}=10599598107.$$
Also,
$$600782\cdot17643=10599596826<V_D,$$
so the surplus is $1281$, and $600782>17642$. Direct calculation gives
$$q=17642-87=17555$$
and
$$E_D=(202-1)(2\cdot17642-87\cdot202)=3559710.$$

Finally,
$$147457-1=2^{14}\cdot3^2.$$
The modular certificates are
$$10^{147456}\equiv1\pmod{147457},\qquad 10^{73728}\equiv-1\pmod{147457},\qquad 10^{49152}\equiv78348\pmod{147457},$$
with
$$\gcd(10^{73728}-1,147457)=\gcd(10^{49152}-1,147457)=1.$$
Pocklington's criterion therefore proves that $147457$ is prime.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $m=2$, $p=147457$, $d=87$, $D=17642$, and $r=600782$. Then $p$ is prime, the affine plane $F_{147457}^2$ has
$$\Lambda=p(p+1)=21743714306$$
affine lines and
$$N=p^2(p+1)=3206262880419842$$
point-line incidences, and the space of polynomials in $F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $17642$ has dimension
$$V_D=10599598107.$$
Moreover,
$$r(D+1)=10599596826,
\qquad V_D-r(D+1)=1281,
\qquad r>D,$$
$$\left\lfloor\frac{D}{d}\right\rfloor=202,
\qquad q=D-d=17555,$$
and
$$E_D=(202-1)(2D-d\cdot202)=3559710.$$
lemmas.title: Fixed arithmetic

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $p=147457$, $P=p+1=147458$, $\Lambda=pP$, $r=600782$, and $j=51837$. For a point of accepted degree $a$, exact-size sampling misses its entire accepted pencil with probability
$$H_a=\frac{\binom{\Lambda-a}{r}}{\binom{\Lambda}{r}}.$$
Consequently, with $\phi_a=aH_a$ and accepted point degrees $a_x$,
$$\mathbb E_R[U_R]=\sum_x\phi_{a_x},
\qquad p^{-2}\sum_xa_x=PA.$$

Set $\Delta_a=\phi_{a+1}-\phi_a$. Direct cancellation gives
$$\Delta_a=H_a\frac{\Lambda-a-(a+1)r}{\Lambda-a}$$
and
$$\Delta_{a+1}-\Delta_a
=H_a\frac{r((r+1)a+2r-2\Lambda)}{(\Lambda-a)(\Lambda-a-1)}.$$
Thus the increments decrease and then increase exactly once.

Let $\rho=H_P/H_j$. The chord joining $(j,\phi_j)$ and $(P,\phi_P)$ is a global upper majorant when
$$\frac{114159961430283}{1603138490176901}
\le\rho\le
\frac{28543278455889}{400773548798638}.$$
The ratio $\rho$ is a product of $P-j=95621$ factors, each between
$$1-\frac r{\Lambda-P+1}$$
and
$$1-\frac r{\Lambda-j}.$$
Odd and even binomial truncations of orders $15$ and $16$ give
$$\frac{71213}{10^6}<\rho<\frac{14243}{200000}.$$
These bounds lie strictly inside the two tangency thresholds because
$$\frac{71213}{10^6}-\frac{114159961430283}{1603138490176901}
=\frac{4339870684650913}{1603138490176901000000}>0$$
and
$$\frac{28543278455889}{400773548798638}-\frac{14243}{200000}
=\frac{219017819399483}{40077354879863800000}>0.$$
To the left of $j$, every increment is at least the chord slope. To the right, the difference between $\Delta_a$ and that slope first decreases and then increases; its cumulative sum begins nonpositive and returns to zero at $P$, so it cannot become positive earlier. The chord is therefore a global upper majorant.

For the endpoint estimates, set
$$x=\frac r\Lambda,
\qquad c_0=\frac r{\Lambda-r},$$
$$J_1=\frac{a(a-1)}2,
\qquad J_2=\frac{a(a-1)(2a-1)}6,$$
$$T_a=c_0\left(\frac{J_1}{\Lambda}+\frac{J_2}{\Lambda^2}\right),
\qquad R_a=\frac{c_0J_1}{\Lambda-a+1}.$$
Writing the factors defining $H_a$ as $(1-x)(1-u_i)$ gives
$$\sum_i u_i\ge T_a,
\qquad \sum_i u_i\le R_a,$$
and hence
$$\prod_i(1-u_i)
\le\exp\left(-\sum_i u_i\right)
\le1-T_a+\frac{R_a^2}{2}.$$
Even binomial truncations for $(1-x)^a$, of order $20$ at $a=j$ and order $30$ at $a=P$, certify
$$H_j<h_j:=\frac{238762637131533}{10^{15}}$$
and
$$H_P<h_P:=\frac{17003158362223}{10^{15}}.$$

The chord has negative slope. Averaging it at the known mean degree $PA$, using $A\ge\epsilon$ and $\epsilon P>j$, yields
$$\frac{\mathbb E_R[U_R]}N
<\frac{j(1-\epsilon)h_j+(\epsilon P-j)h_P}{P-j}
=\delta_{\mathrm{energy}}.$$
Some set $R$ of exactly $600782$ lines therefore satisfies the asserted strict bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $G$ be the accepted incidence graph of the degree-$87$ affine line-versus-point test on $F_{147457}^2$, let $E$ be its edge set, and let
$$N=3206262880419842,
\qquad A=\frac{|E|}{N},
\qquad \epsilon=\frac{359229046020947}{10^{15}}.$$
If $A\ge\epsilon$, then there exists a set $R$ of exactly $600782$ affine lines such that, if $U_R$ denotes the number of accepted incidences whose point has no accepted incident line in $R$, then
$$\frac{U_R}{N}<\delta_{\mathrm{energy}},$$
where
$$\delta_{\mathrm{energy}}
=\frac{51837(1-\epsilon)\left(\frac{238762637131533}{10^{15}}\right)
+(147458\epsilon-51837)\left(\frac{17003158362223}{10^{15}}\right)}{95621}.$$
lemmas.title: Whole-pencil energy bound

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For a parametrization $L(t)=(X_L(t),Y_L(t))$, substitution of a polynomial $P_L(t)$ of degree at most $87$ into a polynomial of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $17642$ produces a univariate polynomial of degree at most $17642$. Hence each identity
$$A(L(t),P_L(t))=0$$
imposes at most $17643$ homogeneous linear coefficient constraints. By P1, the weighted monomial space has dimension $10599598107$, whereas all selected lines impose at most
$$600782\cdot17643=10599596826$$
constraints. The homogeneous system therefore has a nonzero solution.

If such a solution were independent of $Z$, it would be a bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $17642$ vanishing formally on $600782>17642$ distinct affine lines. KTZ Lemma 2.5 would make it the zero polynomial, a contradiction. Every nonzero kernel element therefore depends on $Z$. Since
$$\deg_ZA\le\left\lfloor\frac{17642}{87}\right\rfloor=202<147457,$$
this dependence implies $A_Z\ne0$.

Choose a nonzero kernel element of minimum weighted degree. If an irreducible factor $F$ occurred at least twice, write $A=F^2G$. On every selected graph,
$$F(L(t),P_L(t))^2G(L(t),P_L(t))=0$$
in the integral domain $F_{147457}[t]$. Thus either the specialized factor $F$ or the specialized complementary factor $G$ is zero, and in either case
$$(A/F)(L(t),P_L(t))=0.$$
The quotient is a nonzero kernel element, and the preceding application of KTZ Lemma 2.5 shows that it remains $Z$-dependent. Its weighted degree is smaller than that of $A$, contradicting minimality. Hence $A$ is squarefree.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For every set $R$ of $600782$ distinct affine lines in $F_{147457}^2$ and every assignment to each $L\in R$ of a polynomial $P_L\in F_{147457}[t]$ with $\deg P_L\le87$, there exists a nonzero squarefree polynomial
$$A\in F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$$
of $(1,1,87)$-weighted degree at most $17642$ such that
$$A(L(t),P_L(t))=0$$
in $F_{147457}[t]$ for every $L\in R$, and
$$A_Z\ne0.$$
lemmas.title: Weighted interpolant

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Every line in $R$ is an $A$-identity line by P3. Let $L\notin R$, and let $x$ be a hit accepted point on $L$. There is a selected accepted line $M\in R$ through $x$. Acceptance gives
$$P_L(x)=f(x)=P_M(x),$$
while the selected-line identity gives
$$A(x,P_M(x))=0.$$
Thus $A(x,P_L(x))=0$. The restriction $A(L(t),P_L(t))$ has degree at most $D=17642$, so more than $D$ distinct hit accepted points force this restriction to vanish identically. Hence every line in $T$ is an $A$-identity line.

Each line outside $T$ has at most $D$ hit accepted incidences. Every accepted incidence outside $E_T$ that is not hit occurs at a point whose accepted pencil misses $R$, and is therefore counted by $U_R$. Summing these two kinds of incidences over the $\Lambda-|T|$ lines outside $T$ gives
$$|E|\le |E_T|+U_R+D(\Lambda-|T|).$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $R$ and $A$ satisfy the conclusions of P2 and P3. An accepted point on a line $L\notin R$ is hit if its accepted pencil contains a line in $R$. Let $T$ consist of the lines in $R$ together with every line $L\notin R$ having more than $D=17642$ hit accepted points, and let
$$E_T=\{(x,L)\in E:L\in T\}.$$
Then every line in $T$ satisfies the formal identity
$$A(L(t),P_L(t))=0,$$
and
$$|E|\le |E_T|+U_R+D(\Lambda-|T|).$$
lemmas.title: Identity-line accounting

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Write $A=CB$, where $C\in F_{147457}[X,Y]$ is the coefficient content of $A$ in $Z$ and $B$ is primitive. Put
$$h=\deg C,
\qquad W=\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}B,
\qquad \nu=\deg_ZB.$$
Weighted leading forms give
$$h+W=\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}A\le17642.$$
The polynomial $B$ is squarefree and $B_Z\ne0$. Primitivity excludes any $Z$-independent irreducible factor of $B$. Since
$$1\le\nu\le202<147457,$$
every irreducible factor of positive $Z$-degree has nonzero ordinary $Z$-derivative. Reducing $B_Z$ modulo each irreducible factor of the squarefree polynomial $B$ therefore gives
$$\gcd(B,B_Z)=1.$$

A content line makes $C$ vanish identically and hence contributes a distinct affine linear factor of $C$. There are at most $h$ such lines. Suppose next that $\nu\ge2$. The nominal-degree discriminant
$$\operatorname{Disc}_Z(B)$$
is nonzero. Each of its monomials has coefficient degree $2\nu-2$ and coefficient-index weight $\nu(\nu-1)$, so
$$\deg_{X,Y}\operatorname{Disc}_Z(B)
\le(\nu-1)(2W-87\nu).$$

If a noncontent identity line $L$ is derivative-degenerate, then over $F_{147457}(t)$ the nominal-degree homogenization of $B(L(t),Z)$ has the repeated finite root $[P_L(t):1]$. Since $\nu<147457$, the scalar $\nu$ is nonzero, and Euler's identity makes this point singular. Thus the specialized nominal-degree discriminant vanishes, even if the leading coefficient specializes to zero; no leading coefficient is divided by. The line $L$ consequently divides the discriminant. Therefore
$$e\le h+(\nu-1)(2W-87\nu).$$
Under $h+W\le17642$ and $\nu\le202$, the right-hand side is maximized at $h=0$ and $\nu=202$, giving
$$e\le(202-1)(2\cdot17642-87\cdot202)=3559710.$$
When $\nu=1$, a derivative-degenerate noncontent line would divide both coefficients of the primitive polynomial $B$, which is impossible.

On a nonexceptional identity line, $C(L(t))$ is nonzero. Since
$$C(L(t))B(L(t),P_L(t))=0$$
in the domain $F_{147457}[t]$, the restriction of $B$ vanishes identically. Its derivative restriction is nonzero and has degree at most
$$W-87\le17642-87=17555,$$
so it has at most $17555$ roots.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For the polynomial $A$ and identity-line set $T$ of P3-P4, write
$$A=CB,$$
where $C\in F_{147457}[X,Y]$ is the coefficient content in $Z$ and $B\in F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ is primitive. Call $L\in T$ a content line if $C(L(t))=0$ identically, and call a noncontent line derivative-degenerate if
$$B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))=0$$
identically. If $e$ is the number of content or derivative-degenerate identity lines, then
$$e\le3559710.$$
For every other line $L\in T$,
$$B(L(t),P_L(t))=0,$$
and $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $17555$, hence has at most $17555$ roots in $F_{147457}$.
lemmas.title: Primitive discriminant cleanup

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put
$$t=|T|,
\qquad e=|\mathcal E|,
\qquad q=17555,
\qquad D=17642,
\qquad s=5495.$$
Suppose the deletion process empties the graph. Charge every edge at its earliest deletion. Exceptional lines contribute at most $pe$ edges. By P5, derivative-zero deletions on the other $t-e$ identity lines contribute at most $q(t-e)$. Each of the $p^2$ point vertices contributes at most $D$ edges when peeled, and each of the $t-e$ nonexceptional line vertices contributes at most $s-1=5494$ edges when peeled. Hence
$$|E_T|\le pe+q(t-e)+Dp^2+(s-1)(t-e).$$
Combining this with P4 gives
$$|E|\le U_R+D\Lambda+Dp^2+(s-88)t+(p-q-s+1)e.$$
Here
$$s-88=5407>0$$
and
$$p-q-s+1=124408>0.$$
Using $t\le\Lambda$ and $e\le E_D=3559710$ therefore yields
$$|E|\le U_R+C_0,$$
where
$$C_0=Dp^2+(q+s-1)\Lambda+(p-q-s+1)E_D.$$
The three charges are
$$Dp^2=383600006350058,$$
$$(q+s-1)\Lambda=501170871038994,$$
and
$$(p-q-s+1)E_D=442856401680.$$
Thus
$$C_0=885213733790732$$
and
$$\frac{C_0}{N}=\frac{442606866895366}{1603131440209921}.$$
By P2,
$$\frac{U_R}{N}<\delta_{\mathrm{energy}}.$$
The exact remaining margin is
$$\epsilon-\frac{C_0}{N}-\delta_{\mathrm{energy}}
=\frac{67333805766276738068309588974841569}{153293031444312855941000000000000000000000000000000}>0.$$
Consequently, complete deletion would imply $|E|/N<\epsilon$, contrary to the hypothesis. The core is nonempty. The peeling thresholds give minimum point degree $D+1=17643$ and minimum line degree $s=5495$. Exceptional lines and derivative-zero incidences were removed, so every retained line has a formal $B$-identity and every retained edge satisfies $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let an accepted incidence graph for the degree-$87$ test on $F_{147457}^2$ have acceptance at least
$$\epsilon=\frac{359229046020947}{10^{15}}.$$
Choose $R$, $T$, and $B$ as in P2, P4, and P5. Delete all accepted edges on the exceptional lines, delete every accepted incidence $(x,L)$ on the other identity lines for which
$$B_Z(x,f(x))=0,$$
and then iteratively delete point vertices of current degree at most $17642$ and line vertices of current degree at most $5494$. The resulting core is nonempty, every retained point has degree at least $17643$, every retained line has degree at least $5495$ and satisfies
$$B(L(t),P_L(t))=0,$$
and every retained edge $(x,L)$ satisfies
$$B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0.$$
lemmas.title: Core survival

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For each affine line $L$, put $n_L=|X\cap L|$. Every point lies on $p+1$ lines, so
$$\sum_Ln_L=(p+1)|X|.$$
For the second moment, every ordered pair of distinct points determines exactly one affine line, while each diagonal ordered pair lies on $p+1$ lines. Hence
$$\sum_Ln_L^2=|X|^2+p|X|.$$
Since the average value of $n_L$ is $ap$, expansion gives
$$\sum_L(n_L-ap)^2=p^3a(1-a).$$

The centered indicator of $S$ has squared norm
$$\sum_L(1_S(L)-b)^2=p(p+1)b(1-b).$$
Moreover,
$$I(X,S)-abN
=\sum_L(1_S(L)-b)(n_L-ap).$$
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore gives
$$I(X,S)-abN
\le p^2\sqrt{(p+1)a(1-a)b(1-b)}.$$
Dividing by $N=p^2(p+1)$ proves the bound.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $X\subseteq F_{147457}^2$ have density
$$a=\frac{|X|}{147457^2},$$
and let $S$ be a set of affine lines of density
$$b=\frac{|S|}{147457\cdot147458}.$$
If
$$I(X,S)=|\{(x,L)\in X\times S:x\in L\}|$$
and
$$N=147457^2\cdot147458,$$
then
$$\frac{I(X,S)}N
\le ab+\sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)b(1-b)}{147458}}.$$
lemmas.title: Affine incidence mixing

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Fix a component, and let $a$ and $b$ be its point and line densities. Let $\eta$ be its retained-edge count normalized by
$$N=147457^2\cdot147458.$$
The minimum degrees from P6 give
$$\eta\ge\alpha a,
\qquad \eta\ge\beta b,$$
where
$$\alpha=\frac{17643}{147458},
\qquad \beta=\frac{5495}{147457}.$$
Put
$$c=\frac\alpha\beta
=\frac{2601583851}{810281710}$$
and
$$\gamma^2=\frac1{147458c}
=\frac{5495}{2601583851}.$$

Suppose $ca<1/2$. If $b\le ca$, then $b(1-b)\le ca(1-ca)$. Combining $\eta\ge\alpha a$ with P7 and dividing by $ca$ gives
$$\beta\le a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.$$
If $b\ge ca$, combine $\eta\ge\beta b$ with P7, divide by $b$, and use
$$\frac{1-b}{b}\le\frac{1-ca}{ca}$$
to obtain the same inequality. Thus every such component satisfies
$$\beta\le a+\gamma\sqrt{(1-a)(1-ca)}.$$

Set
$$\tau=\frac{359229046020947}{10^{16}}$$
and
$$F(a)=(\beta-a)^2-\gamma^2(1-a)(1-ca).$$
Exact arithmetic gives
$$\beta-\tau
=\frac{1979162560889218221}{1474570000000000000000}>0$$
and
$$\frac12-c\tau
=\frac{3116844065061768477073103}{8102817100000000000000000}>0.$$
It also gives
$$F(\tau)
=\frac{310822941801540312341284744748980665822691}{5656809599924727240600000000000000000000000000000000}>0,$$
$$F'(\tau)
=-\frac{5132867511958194323768549071}{1918121757503790000000000000000}<0,$$
and
$$F''=2\left(1-\frac1{147458}\right)>0.$$
Hence $F'$ is negative throughout $[0,\tau]$, and therefore
$$F(a)\ge F(\tau)>0$$
for $0\le a\le\tau$. If a nonempty component had $a\le\tau$, then $ca<1/2$ and $\beta-a>0$; squaring the preceding mixing consequence would instead give $F(a)\le0$, a contradiction. Thus $a>\tau$.

Finally,
$$\tau\cdot147457^2
=781092077+\frac{6258958548786003}{10^{16}},$$
so the integral number of point vertices is at least $781092078$.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Every connected component of the retained core constructed in P6 has point density strictly greater than
$$\frac{359229046020947}{10^{16}}.$$
Consequently, every such component contains at least $781092078$ point vertices.
lemmas.title: Component size

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose a point vertex $x_0$ in the component. By P6 it is incident to at least $17643=D+1$ retained lines. Their labels have degree at most $87$, satisfy the formal $B$-identity, and all take the value $f(x_0)$ at $x_0$. This value is a simple root because
$$B_Z(x_0,f(x_0))\ne0.$$
KTZ Lemma 6.1, equivalently its derivation from KTZ Lemmas 2.7 and 2.5, produces a polynomial
$$Q\in F_{147457}[X,Y]$$
of total degree at most $87$ such that
$$B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))=0$$
and such that $Q$ restricts to every retained line through $x_0$.

At every point reached from this initial star, $Q(x)=f(x)$, and P6 ensures that this common root remains simple. On a retained line adjacent to such a point, the restriction of $Q$ and the submitted line polynomial are both degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial roots of the specialized relation $B$ and have the same simple value at the reached point. The one-variable specialization of KTZ Lemma 2.7 makes the two restrictions identical. Thus equality with $f$ propagates across each adjacent retained line. Connectivity propagates the same fixed polynomial $Q$ throughout the component.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For every connected component $\mathcal C$ of the retained core constructed in P6, there exists a polynomial
$$Q\in F_{147457}[X,Y]$$
of total degree at most $87$ such that
$$Q(x)=f(x)$$
for every point vertex $x$ of $\mathcal C$.
lemmas.title: Component polynomial

lemmas.proof_markdown:
By P6, the retained core is nonempty, so it has a connected component. By P8, that component has point density strictly greater than $359229046020947/10^{16}$. By P9, one polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$ agrees with $f$ at every point of the component. Therefore its agreement probability is greater than, and hence at least, $359229046020947/10^{16}$.

The current doubly verified score is $7099751645463/10^{13}$. The exact subtraction
$$7099751645463/10^{13}-359229046020947/10^{15}=350746118525353/10^{15}>0$$
shows that the asserted soundness value is strictly smaller.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For every function
$$f:F_{147457}^2\to F_{147457}$$
and every assignment of a univariate polynomial $P_L$ of degree at most $87$ to each affine line $L$, if the uniform affine-line-then-point verifier accepts with probability at least
$$359229046020947/10^{15},$$
then there exists
$$Q\in F_{147457}[X,Y]$$
of total degree at most $87$ such that
$$\Pr_{x\in F_{147457}^2}[Q(x)=f(x)]\ge359229046020947/10^{16}.$$
Moreover,
$$7099751645463/10^{13}-359229046020947/10^{15}=350746118525353/10^{15}>0.$$
lemmas.title: Soundness conclusion

lemmas.proof_markdown: Two distinct points of $F_{147457}^2$ determine exactly one affine line. A copy of $K_{2,2}$ would require two distinct point vertices to have two distinct common line neighbors. This is impossible.
lemmas.statement_markdown: The affine point-line incidence graph of $F_{147457}^2$ contains no subgraph isomorphic to $K_{2,2}$.
lemmas.title: Incidence obstruction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Each point $x$ is incident to exactly $147458$ affine lines. Choose any $a_x$ of its incident edges. Choices made at distinct point vertices concern distinct incidence edges, so they can be made independently. The union of all chosen edges has point degree exactly $a_x$ at every $x$.

Consequently, mixtures supported on the endpoints of an upper-concave-envelope chord can realize the associated point-degree linear program up to integer rounding. Thus point-degree moments alone cannot improve the whole-pencil bound without additional line-side or polynomial-label information.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For every family of integers
$$(a_x)_{x\in F_{147457}^2}$$
satisfying
$$0\le a_x\le147458$$
for every $x$, there exists a subgraph of the affine point-line incidence graph of $F_{147457}^2$ in which the degree of each point vertex $x$ is exactly $a_x$.
lemmas.title: Degree-sequence realization

lemmas.proof_markdown: Set $p=147457$, $P=p^2=21743566849$, and $\Lambda=p(p+1)=21743714306$. Follow a valid low-degree deletion order until exactly $35585$ point vertices or exactly $23401$ line vertices remain. After either boundary is reached, delete arbitrary opposite-side vertices until exactly $35585$ points and $23401$ lines remain; their degrees cannot exceed the corresponding deletion thresholds. Charge every edge to its earliest deleted endpoint. If $I$ is the number of incidences between the remaining vertices, then $|E(G)|\le23401(P-35585)+35585(\Lambda-23401)+I$. For each remaining point $x$, let $r_x$ be its degree among the remaining lines. Since two distinct affine lines meet in at most one point, $\sum_x\binom{r_x}{2}\le\binom{23401}{2}=273791700$. If $I=4432061$, then $I=124\cdot35585+19521$, and convexity gives $\sum_x\binom{r_x}{2}\ge35585\binom{124}{2}+19521\cdot124=273791814>273791700$, a contradiction. Hence $I\le4432060$. Substitution yields $|E(G)|\le23401P+35585\Lambda-2(23401)(35585)+4432060=1282569620395349$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G$ be a subgraph of the affine point-line incidence graph of $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. If iterative deletion of point vertices of current degree at most $23401$ and line vertices of current degree at most $35585$ deletes every vertex of $G$, then $|E(G)|\le1282569620395349$.
lemmas.title: Geometric empty-core bound

lemmas.proof_markdown: There are $N=p^2(p+1)=3206262880419842$ affine point-line incidences. Exact arithmetic gives $40002010696871N=10^{14}\cdot1282569620395349+43623475714382$. Thus the acceptance hypothesis and integrality of the accepted-edge count imply $|E(G_{\mathrm{acc}})|\ge1282569620395350$. This exceeds the empty-core cap in [P1], so the deletion process cannot empty the graph. Every vertex remaining at termination has point degree at least $23402$ or line degree at least $35586$, respectively.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For the fixed parameters $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, let $G_{\mathrm{acc}}$ be the accepted-incidence graph of a point table and an affine-line label table. If $\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge40002010696871/10^{14}$, then the core obtained by deleting point vertices of degree at most $23401$ and line vertices of degree at most $35585$ is nonempty and has minimum point and line degrees at least $23402$ and $35586$, respectively.
lemmas.title: First-core survival

lemmas.proof_markdown: Set $p=147457$, and let $x$ and $n$ denote the point- and line-vertex counts. Affine incidence second moments and centered Cauchy–Schwarz give $I(x,n)\le xn/p+\sqrt{pxn}$. If $x\ge n$, the point minimum degree implies $23402\le n/p+\sqrt{pn/x}<n/p+385$. If $n\ge x$, the line minimum degree gives the stronger analogous inequality $35586\le x/p+\sqrt{px/n}<x/p+385$. Since $384^2=147456<p<385^2$, both cases imply $x,n>p(23402-385)=3394017769$. Their integrality therefore gives $x,n\ge3394017770$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G$ be a nonempty subgraph of the affine point-line incidence graph of $\mathbb F_{147457}^2$. If its minimum point degree is at least $23402$ and its minimum line degree is at least $35586$, then $G$ has at least $3394017770$ point vertices and at least $3394017770$ line vertices.
lemmas.title: First-core vertex mass

lemmas.proof_markdown: Select every line of the first core independently with probability $\theta=2269269/46802000000$. Each accepted point on a fixed core line has at least $23401$ alternative core lines. Alternative-line sets belonging to distinct points of the fixed line are disjoint, so their coverage indicators are independent. Each success probability exceeds $1-\exp(-23401\theta)=1-\exp(-2269269/2000000)>\rho$, where $\rho=67846035/10^8$; the last inequality follows from the exact degree-$10$ Taylor certificate $\sum_{j=0}^{10}(2269269/2000000)^j/j!>10^8/32153965$. For a core line with $m\ge35586$ accepted points, Hoeffding's lower-tail inequality gives $\Pr[\text{covered points}\le23401]<\exp(-2(\rho m-23401)^2/m)<\exp(-31)$. At the endpoint, $2(67846035\cdot35586-10^8\cdot23401)^2-31\cdot10^{16}\cdot35586=109170584764560200>0$, and the exponent increases thereafter. Exact rational estimates give $\Lambda\exp(-31)<751/10^6$, so all core lines are covered successfully with probability greater than $999249/10^6$. For $r=1055070$, Markov's inequality gives $\Pr[|R|\le r]\ge1-\theta\Lambda/(r+1)=1091062427579/1452336263000000>751/10^6$. The two good-event probabilities sum to more than $1$, so some selected family satisfies both conclusions. Finally, an alternative affine line meets a fixed line in at most one point; covering $23402$ distinct points therefore requires at least $23402$ selected lines.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_0$ be the first core supplied by [P2]. There exists a subset $R$ of its line vertices with $23402\le|R|\le1055070$ such that, for every line vertex $L$ of $G_0$, at least $23402$ accepted point vertices of $L$ are incident with lines in $R\setminus\{L\}$.
lemmas.title: Sparse reaching family

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The number of monomials in the weighted region is $M=\sum_{k=0}^{268} inom{23401-87k+2}{2}=24690750075$. On each selected line, the graph-point evaluations of a restriction of degree at most $23401$ impose at most $23402$ independent homogeneous linear conditions. Thus all selected lines impose at most $1055070\cdot23402=24690748140$ conditions, leaving surplus $1935$, and a nonzero interpolant exists. A $Z$-independent interpolant would have at least $23402$ distinct affine-line factors while having total degree at most $23401$, which is impossible. Hence the interpolant depends on $Z$. Its weighted-degree bound gives $\deg_ZA\le268<147457$, so $A_Z
ot\equiv0$. Choose an interpolant of minimum weighted degree among those having nonzero $Z$-derivative. If $A=F^eG$, where $e\ge2$, $F$ is irreducible, and $F
mid G$, then $FG$ still vanishes at every selected graph point. If $(FG)_Z\equiv0$, reduction modulo $F$ gives $F\mid F_Z$. Hence $F_Z\equiv0$, and then $G_Z\equiv0$, contradicting $A_Z
ot\equiv0$. Therefore $(FG)_Z
ot\equiv0$, contradicting the minimality of $A$. Thus $A$ is squarefree. Finally, every selected-line restriction has degree at most $23401<147457$ and vanishes at all $147457$ graph points, so it is identically zero.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $R$ be a selected line family satisfying [P4], and give $X,Y,Z$ weights $1,1,87$. There exists a squarefree polynomial $A\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$ of weighted degree at most $23401$ such that $A_Z\not\equiv0$ and $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ for every $L\in R$.
lemmas.title: Weighted squarefree interpolant

lemmas.proof_markdown: Fix a first-core line $L$. By [P4], it contains at least $23402$ distinct accepted points, each lying on a selected alternative line $L'$. At such an intersection $x$, both accepted labels equal $f(x)$, while [P5] gives $A(x,P_{L'}(x))=0$. Hence $A(x,P_L(x))=0$. The polynomial $A(L(t),P_L(t))$ has degree at most $23401$ and at least $23402$ distinct roots, so it is identically zero.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_0$, $R$, and $A$ satisfy [P4] and [P5]. For every line vertex $L$ of $G_0$, $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$.
lemmas.title: Core-line interpolation identity

lemmas.proof_markdown: View $A$ as a polynomial in $Z$ over $\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$. Let $H$ be its coefficient content and write $A=HB$, with $B$ primitive in $Z$. Put $D=23401$, $h=\deg H$, $W=\operatorname{wdeg}_{(1,1,87)}B$, and $n=\deg_ZB$. Highest weighted parts multiply nontrivially, so $h+W\le D$. Every irreducible factor of $B$ has positive $Z$-degree. Since $B$ is squarefree and $n\le268<147457$, $\gcd(B,B_Z)=1$. Suppose first that $n\ge2$. The nonzero nominal-degree discriminant $\Delta_Z(B)$ is homogeneous of coefficient degree $2n-2$ and coefficient-index weight $n(n-1)$; consequently, $\deg_{X,Y}\Delta_Z(B)\le(n-1)(2W-87n)$. At most $h$ affine lines divide $H$. On every other first-core line, $A(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$ implies $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$. If also $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, then $P_L$ is a repeated finite root over $\mathbb F_{147457}(t)$. The nominal binary homogenization therefore has a repeated projective root even if its leading coefficient specializes to zero, so the line form divides $\Delta_Z(B)$; no leading coefficient is inverted. The number of content and derivative-degenerate lines is at most $h+(n-1)(2W-87n)\le(n-1)(2D-87n)$. This last expression increases for $2\le n\le268$ and reaches $(268-1)(2\cdot23401-87\cdot268)=6270762$. If $n=1$, primitivity excludes derivative-degenerate noncontent lines, while $h\le D-87<6270762$. On every remaining line, differentiating in $Z$ lowers weighted degree by $87$, so $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))$ is nonzero and has degree at most $W-87\le D-87=23314$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $A$ satisfy [P5] and [P6]. There exist a factor $B$ of $A$ that is primitive in $Z$ and a set $\mathcal E$ of at most $6270762$ first-core lines such that every first-core line $L\notin\mathcal E$ satisfies $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, while $B_Z(L(t),P_L(t))\not\equiv0$ and $\deg_tB_Z(L(t),P_L(t))\le23314$.
lemmas.title: Primitive discriminant cleanup

lemmas.proof_markdown: Let $x$ and $n$ be the point- and line-vertex counts of the first core, and let $e\le6270762$ be its exceptional-line count. Set $p=147457$, $P=p^2$, $\Lambda=p(p+1)$, and $B_0=23401P+35585\Lambda=1282571281412459$. Suppose cleanup followed by the second peel empties the graph. Charging every accepted edge when it is first removed gives $|E_{\mathrm{acc}}|\le23401(P-x)+35585(\Lambda-n)+pe+23314(n-e)+23401x+6074(n-e)=B_0-6197n+118069e$. By [P3] and [P7], $6197n-118069e\ge6197(3394017770)-118069(6270762)=20292345522112$. Complete deletion would therefore imply $|E_{\mathrm{acc}}|\le B_0-20292345522112=1262278935890347$. But $B_{\mathrm{geom}}=1282569620395349$ and $B_{\mathrm{geom}}-1262278935890347=20290684505002>0$, contradicting [P2]. Thus the second peel leaves a nonempty graph, and its termination conditions give minimum degrees $23402$ and $6075$. By construction and [P7], every retained line satisfies $B(L(t),P_L(t))\equiv0$, and every retained edge $(x,L)$ satisfies $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $G_0$ be the first core supplied by [P2], and let $B$ and the exceptional-line set be supplied by [P7]. Delete every edge incident with an exceptional line and every remaining edge $(x,L)$ satisfying $B_Z(x,f(x))=0$. Iterative deletion of point vertices of current degree at most $23401$ and line vertices of current degree at most $6074$ then leaves a nonempty graph $G_1$ with minimum point degree at least $23402$ and minimum line degree at least $6075$.
lemmas.title: Amortized second-core survival

lemmas.proof_markdown: For each affine line $L$, put $n_L=|X\cap L|$. Counting incidences gives $\sum_Ln_L=(p+1)|X|$. Counting ordered pairs of points of $X$ on a common line gives $\sum_Ln_L^2=|X|^2+p|X|$: each diagonal pair lies on $p+1$ lines, while each ordered pair of distinct points determines one line. Since the average of $n_L$ is $|X|/p=ap$, these identities yield $\sum_L(n_L-ap)^2=p^3a(1-a)$. For $y_L=\mathbf 1_{\mathcal T}(L)$, one has $\sum_L(y_L-b)^2=p(p+1)b(1-b)$. Centering both factors gives $J-ab=\frac{1}{p^2(p+1)}\sum_L(y_L-b)(n_L-ap)$. Cauchy–Schwarz now yields $|J-ab|\le\frac{\sqrt{p(p+1)b(1-b)}\sqrt{p^3a(1-a)}}{p^2(p+1)}=\sqrt{a(1-a)b(1-b)/(p+1)}$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $p=147457$, let $X\subseteq\mathbb F_p^2$, and let $\mathcal T$ be a set of affine lines in $\mathbb F_p^2$. Define $a=|X|/p^2$, $b=|\mathcal T|/(p(p+1))$, and $J=|\{(x,L)\in X\times\mathcal T:x\in L\}|/(p^2(p+1))$. Then $|J-ab|\le\sqrt{a(1-a)b(1-b)/(p+1)}$.
lemmas.title: Centered affine incidence bound

lemmas.proof_markdown: Set $p=147457$. For a component, let $a$ and $b$ be its point and affine-line densities, and let $u$ be its retained-edge count normalized by $p^2(p+1)$. Put $\alpha=23402/(p+1)$, $\beta=6075/p$, $c=\alpha/\beta=23402p/(6075(p+1))$, and $\gamma^2=6075/(23402p)=1/(c(p+1))$. The minimum-degree conditions imply $u\ge\alpha a$ and $u\ge\beta b$, while [P9] gives $u\le U_a(b):=ab+\sqrt{a(1-a)b(1-b)/(p+1)}$. Suppose $a<\beta$ and $ca<1/2$, and set $b_0=ca$. If $F(a):=(\beta-a)^2-\gamma^2(1-a)(1-ca)>0$, then $U_a(b_0)<\alpha a$. Since $U_a(b)$ is increasing below $b_0$ and $U_a(b)/b$ is decreasing above $b_0$, one of the two minimum-degree lower bounds fails for every $b$. Thus feasibility requires $F(a)\le0$. Let $\tau_0=40002062502265/10^{15}$. At $\tau_0$, after clearing positive denominators, the numerator of $F(\tau_0)$ is $129569315454799177169885256289211256171850>0$. The exact estimates $\beta-\tau_0>1/1000$, $c<4$, and $\gamma^2<1/500000$ ensure $a<\beta$ and $ca<1/2$ for $0\le a\le\tau_0$, and give $F'(a)=2(a-\beta)+\gamma^2(1+c-2ca)<-199/100000$ throughout that interval. Hence $F(a)\ge F(\tau_0)>0$ for every $a\le\tau_0$, contradicting feasibility. Therefore $a>\tau_0$. Finally, $40002062502265p^2=869787520\cdot10^{15}+115875241412985$. Since the remainder is positive and the component size is integral, the component contains at least $869787521$ points.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $C$ be a connected component of the graph $G_1$ supplied by [P8], and let $X_C$ be its point-vertex set. Then $|X_C|/147457^2>40002062502265/10^{15}$ and $|X_C|\ge869787521$.
lemmas.title: Component point mass

lemmas.proof_markdown: Put $D=23401$ and choose a point $x_0$ in the component. It lies on at least $23402=D+1$ retained lines; all corresponding labels take the common value $f(x_0)$, and $B_Z(x_0,f(x_0))\ne0$. In formal coordinates around $x_0$, solve $B(X,Y,q)=0$ recursively with constant term $f(x_0)$. At each homogeneous degree, the only division is by the nonzero scalar $B_Z(x_0,f(x_0))$, so the formal solution is unique. Let $Q$ be its total-degree-at-most-$87$ truncation. On every seed line, the formal solution equals the degree-at-most-$87$ line label by one-variable simple-root uniqueness, so $Q|_L=P_L$. The weighted-degree bound for $B$ implies that $B(X,Y,Q)$ has total degree at most $D$. It vanishes on at least $D+1$ distinct seed lines; otherwise their line forms would provide more than $D$ factors. Hence $B(X,Y,Q)\equiv0$ globally. Suppose propagation has reached a retained point $x$, so $Q(x)=f(x)$. On every adjacent retained line, $Q|_L$ and $P_L$ solve the same polynomial identity, take the same value at $x$, and this value is simple because $B_Z(x,f(x))\ne0$. Formal uniqueness makes the two restrictions identical. Every retained edge is accepted, and connectivity therefore propagates $Q=f$ to every point vertex of the component.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $C$ be a connected component of the graph $G_1$ supplied by [P8]. There exists a polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that $Q(x)=f(x)$ for every point vertex $x$ of $C$.
lemmas.title: Component reconstruction

lemmas.proof_markdown: Choose any connected component of the nonempty graph $G_1$. By [P11], one polynomial $Q\in\mathbb F_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ agrees with $f$ at every point of that component. By [P10], its agreement density is greater than $40002062502265/10^{15}$. The excess over the required density is $(40002062502265-40002010696871)/10^{15}=51805394/10^{15}>0$. Consequently, $\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)>40002010696871/10^{15}$. Writing $\varepsilon_0=40002010696871/10^{14}$, this is $\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)>\varepsilon_0/10$. For benchmark comparison, $0.7099751645463-0.40002010696871=0.30995505757759>0$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: For the fixed parameters $m=2$, $p=147457$, and total degree $d=87$, let $f:\mathbb F_{147457}^2\to\mathbb F_{147457}$ and assign a degree-at-most-$87$ univariate polynomial $P_L$ to every affine line $L$. If $\operatorname{Pass}(f,P)\ge40002010696871/10^{14}$, then $\operatorname{Agr}_{87}(f)>40002010696871/10^{15}$.
lemmas.title: Fixed-instance soundness

lemmas.proof_markdown:
There are $147458$ projective directions, and the uniform affine-line-then-point sampler is equivalently obtained by first choosing a uniform direction and then a uniform point. Hence

$$(1/147458)\sum_s e_s=1-\operatorname{Pass}\le 1817/147457.$$

Choose the two smallest directional errors and denote their directions by $u$ and $v$, ordered so that $e_u\le e_v$. The smaller error does not exceed the mean, and the sum of the two smallest errors does not exceed twice the mean. Thus $e_u\le1817/147457$ and $e_u+e_v\le3634/147457$.

Distinct projective directions in $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$ are linearly independent, so an invertible linear change of coordinates sends $u$ and $v$ to the horizontal and vertical directions. Such a change preserves total degree, uniform sampling, and agreement.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$, and assign to every affine line $L\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$ a polynomial label $P_L$ of degree at most $87$. For every projective direction $s$, let $g_s(x)$ be the value at $x$ of the label on the unique line of direction $s$ through $x$, and set $e_s=\Pr_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}}[g_s(x)\ne f(x)]$. If $\Pr_{L,\,x\in L}[P_L(x)=f(x)]\ge145640/147457$, then there are distinct directions $u$ and $v$ such that $e_u\le1817/147457$ and $e_u+e_v\le3634/147457$.
lemmas.title: Directional normalization

lemmas.proof_markdown:
At every cell $(x,y)$ for which $R_y(x)\ne C_x(y)$, at least one of $R_y(x)$ and $C_x(y)$ differs from $f(x,y)$. Therefore the fraction of row-column inconsistent cells is at most $e_u+e_v$. It follows that

$$(1/147457)\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}}G_y\ge147457(1-e_u-e_v)\ge147457-3634=143823.$$

This is the sole union bound converting the two directional errors into row-column inconsistency.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Assume the directions $u$ and $v$ from $P1$ have been sent to the horizontal and vertical directions. Write their degree-at-most-$87$ labels as $R_y(X)$ and $C_x(Y)$, respectively, and define

$$G_y=\left|\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}:R_y(x)=C_x(y)\}\right|.$$

Then $(1/147457)\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}}G_y\ge143823$.
lemmas.title: Two-view consistency

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose uniformly an $88$-element subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{147457}$. Let $\ell_s(X)$ be the Lagrange basis polynomial associated with $s\in S$, and set

$$Q_S(X,Y)=\sum_{s\in S}\ell_s(X)C_s(Y).$$

Every interpolation denominator is a difference of distinct field elements and is therefore nonzero. The polynomial $Q_S$ has degree at most $87$ separately in $X$ and $Y$. If $S\subseteq\{x:R_y(x)=C_x(y)\}$, then $Q_S(X,y)$ and $R_y(X)$ are degree-at-most-$87$ polynomials agreeing at the $88$ points of $S$, so they are identical.

Let $U_y=|\{x:R_y(x)\ne f(x,y)\}|$. A row is copied with probability $\binom{G_y}{88}/\binom{147457}{88}$. On a copied row, $Q_S$ equals $R_y$; subtracting all row-label errors, including those on rows that are not copied, gives

$$\mathbb{E}_S[\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q_S)]\ge (1/147457)\sum_y\frac{\binom{G_y}{88}}{\binom{147457}{88}}-e_u.$$

The integer function $g\mapsto\binom{g}{88}$ is increasing, and its second forward difference is $\binom{g}{86}$. Its piecewise-linear extension is therefore convex. The mean bound from $P2$ yields

$$\mathbb{E}_S[\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q_S)]\ge\frac{\binom{143823}{88}}{\binom{147457}{88}}-e_u\ge\frac{\binom{143823}{88}}{\binom{147457}{88}}-1817/147457.$$

Some choice of $S$ attains at least this expectation.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$, and let $R_y(X)$ and $C_x(Y)$ be degree-at-most-$87$ row and column labels. Suppose

$$e_u=\Pr_{(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}}[R_y(x)\ne f(x,y)]\le1817/147457$$

and, for $G_y=|\{x:R_y(x)=C_x(y)\}|$, suppose $(1/147457)\sum_yG_y\ge143823$. Then there exists $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ with degree at most $87$ separately in $X$ and $Y$ such that

$$\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)\ge\frac{\binom{143823}{88}}{\binom{147457}{88}}-1817/147457.$$
lemmas.title: Bidegree interpolation

lemmas.statement_markdown: Under the hypotheses of $P3$, there exists $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ with degree at most $87$ separately in $X$ and $Y$ such that $\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)>14564/147457$.
lemmas.title: Anchor survival

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The bidegree bound gives $\deg Q\le174$. Suppose that the top total degree is $T$ with $88\le T\le174$, and let $H_T$ be the nonzero homogeneous part of degree $T$. A nonzero binary homogeneous form of degree $T$ vanishes on at most $T$ projective directions. Thus $H_T$ is nonzero on at least $147458-T$ directions.

For each such direction, the restriction of $Q$ to every affine line has exact degree $T$. Its difference from the supplied degree-at-most-$87$ label has exact degree $T<147457$ and hence at most $T$ roots. Therefore

$$\Pr_x[Q(x)=g_s(x)]\le T/147457.$$

The simultaneous events $Q(x)=f(x)$ and $g_s(x)=f(x)$ imply $Q(x)=g_s(x)$. Hence, on every such direction,

$$e_s>14564/147457-T/147457\ge14390/147457>9/100,$$

where the last strict inequality follows from

$$100\cdot14390-9\cdot147457=111887>0.$$

The fraction of directions on which this holds is at least $(147458-T)/147458$, which is at least $(147458-174)/147458>99/100$ because

$$100(147458-174)-99(147458)=130058>0.$$

Consequently, the mean directional error is greater than

$$(99/100)(9/100)=891/10000>1817/147457,$$

where

$$891\cdot147457-10000\cdot1817=113214187>0.$$

This contradicts the acceptance hypothesis. Therefore the top total degree is at most $87$.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$ and let every affine line carry a degree-at-most-$87$ label. Suppose the line-versus-point acceptance is at least $145640/147457$. If $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ has degree at most $87$ separately in $X$ and $Y$ and satisfies $\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)>14564/147457$, then $Q$ has total degree at most $87$.
lemmas.title: Total-degree elimination

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Apply $P1$ to normalize two selected directions, $P2$ to compare their row and column labels, $P3$ and $P4$ to obtain a bidegree-at-most-$(87,87)$ polynomial with agreement strictly greater than $14564/147457$, and $P5$ to show that this polynomial has total degree at most $87$. Undoing the invertible coordinate change preserves total degree and agreement.

The agreement threshold corresponds to

$$(14564/147457)\cdot147457^2=14564\cdot147457=2147563748$$

points. Since the proved agreement is strict and the number of agreeing points is an integer, there are at least $2147563749$ agreeing points.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$, and assign to every affine line a polynomial label of degree at most $87$. If the uniform affine-line-then-point acceptance is at least $145640/147457$, then there exists $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that $\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)>14564/147457$. In particular, $Q$ agrees with $f$ at at least $2147563749$ points.
lemmas.title: Direct soundness

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose coordinates in which the anchor lines have equations $X=a_i$ and the crossing lines have equations $Y=b$. Interpolate the $88$ anchor labels in the $X$ variable. Since the $a_i$ are distinct, all Lagrange denominators are nonzero, and this produces a unique polynomial $Q$ of bidegree at most $(87,87)$ whose restriction to every anchor line is its supplied label.

On a crossing line $Y=b$, both $Q(X,b)$ and the supplied crossing label have degree at most $87$ in $X$. They agree at the $88$ intersections with the anchor lines, so they coincide identically.

On each witness line $M_k$, the restriction of $Q$ has degree at most $174$. It agrees with the degree-at-most-$87$ witness label at its intersections with at least $175$ distinct crossing lines. These intersections are distinct, so the two restrictions coincide.

Write $Q=\sum_{r=0}^{174}H_r$ as a sum of homogeneous parts and descend from $r=174$ to $r=88$. The bidegree bound implies

$$H_r=X^{r-87}Y^{r-87}R_r,$$

where $R_r$ is homogeneous of degree $174-r\le86$. After all higher homogeneous parts have been shown to vanish, the coefficient of parameter degree $r$ on a witness line of direction $v_k$ is $H_r(v_k)$. Since the restriction to $M_k$ has degree at most $87$, this coefficient is zero. The $87$ witness directions are distinct and different from both coordinate directions, so $R_r$ has $87$ distinct projective zeros. As $\deg R_r\le86$, it follows that $R_r=0$. Descending in $r$ eliminates every homogeneous part of degree greater than $87$.

If the stated consistencies arise from simultaneous acceptance against a point table $f$, then every accepted point on a crossing line is an agreement point for the same polynomial $Q$. Because the crossing lines are parallel and distinct, those agreement points add without overlap.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $\mathcal{A}=\{A_0,\ldots,A_{87}\}$ be $88$ distinct parallel affine lines in $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$, let $\mathcal{C}$ be a family of at least $175$ distinct parallel affine lines in a second direction, and let $M_1,\ldots,M_{87}$ have pairwise distinct directions different from those two directions. Suppose every line in $\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{C}\cup\{M_1,\ldots,M_{87}\}$ carries a polynomial label of degree at most $87$, every $A_i$ and every member of $\mathcal{C}$ have consistent labels at their intersection, and each $M_k$ has a label consistent with the labels of at least $175$ distinct members of $\mathcal{C}$ at their intersections. Then there exists $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ whose restriction equals the supplied label on every line in $\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{C}\cup\{M_1,\ldots,M_{87}\}$.
lemmas.title: Anchored gluing

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Choose two directions in $D$ as coordinate axes. Every function on $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$ has a unique reduced polynomial representative whose degree in each variable is at most $147456$. The degree-at-most-$87$ restrictions in the first coordinate direction imply that every coefficient of $X^i$ with $i\ge88$ vanishes at all $147457$ values of the transverse coordinate. Each such coefficient has degree below $147457$, so it is the zero polynomial. Applying the same argument to the second coordinate direction shows that the reduced representative $Q$ has bidegree at most $(87,87)$.

For each of the remaining $87$ directions, the restriction of $Q$ to any affine line has degree at most $174<147457$. It agrees at all $147457$ points of that line with a polynomial of degree at most $87$. Their difference has more roots than its degree and is therefore the zero polynomial, so every such restriction of $Q$ formally has degree at most $87$.

Write $Q=\sum_{r=0}^{174}H_r$ in homogeneous parts and descend from $r=174$ to $r=88$. The bidegree bound gives $H_r=X^{r-87}Y^{r-87}R_r$ with $\deg R_r=174-r\le86$. After the higher parts have vanished, the coefficient of parameter degree $r$ in each of the remaining $87$ directions is $H_r$ evaluated on that direction. It is zero because the corresponding restrictions have degree at most $87$. The directions are distinct and nonaxis, so $R_r$ has $87$ distinct projective roots. Since its degree is at most $86$, $R_r=0$. Thus all homogeneous parts of total degree greater than $87$ vanish.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $D$ be a set of $89$ distinct projective directions in $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$. If $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$ restricts to a polynomial of degree at most $87$ on every affine line in every direction in $D$, then there exists $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ such that $Q(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$.
lemmas.title: Directional rigidity

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The polynomial $H$ is the product of the $88$ distinct linear forms $X$, $Y$, and $Y-m_iX$ for $1\le i\le86$. It is homogeneous of total degree $88$. Its degree in either individual variable is at most $87$.

On a translate of any selected factor direction, the coefficient of parameter degree $88$ is the value of the top homogeneous form on that direction, which is zero because the corresponding linear factor vanishes there. Thus the restriction has degree at most $87$.

For any polynomial $Q$ of total degree at most $87$, the polynomial $H-Q$ is nonzero and has total degree $88$. Its individual degrees are below $147457$, so it cannot vanish on all of $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$. More quantitatively, the bivariate root bound gives at most $88\cdot147457$ zeros. Hence no such $Q$ represents $H$ as a function, and every such $Q$ agrees with $H$ at at most $88\cdot147457$ points.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
For any distinct $m_1,\ldots,m_{86}\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{\times}$, define

$$H(X,Y)=XY\prod_{i=1}^{86}(Y-m_iX).$$

The restriction of $H$ to every affine line in the horizontal, vertical, or slope-$m_i$ directions has degree at most $87$. No polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$ represents $H$ on $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$, and every such polynomial agrees with $H$ at at most $88\cdot147457$ points.
lemmas.title: Directional sharpness

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Regard $B$ as a polynomial in $Z$ over the unique factorization domain $\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$. Eisenstein's criterion at the prime $X$ applies: $X$ divides the constant coefficient $-XY$, $X^2$ does not divide it, and $X$ does not divide the leading coefficient. Thus $B$ is irreducible. It is monic in $Z$ and hence primitive.

The prime $147457$ is odd, so $B_Z=2Z$ is nonzero. Moreover, $\gcd(B,2Z)=1$, and therefore $B$ is squarefree. Under weights $(1,1,87)$, the terms $Z^2$ and $XY$ have weights $174$ and $2$, respectively, so the weighted degree is $174$.

For a nonaxis direction represented by $(1,m)$, a degree-one polynomial $P(t)=ct$ satisfies

$$B(t,mt,P(t))\equiv0$$

exactly when $c^2=m$. There are $(147457-1)/2=73728$ nonzero square slopes. The two coordinate axes additionally carry the root $P(t)=0$. Hence $73730$ distinct pencil lines carry degree-at-most-one roots, all taking the value $0$ at the origin. At that point $B_Z=0$, so the common value is singular.

A global polynomial root would satisfy $Q^2=XY$. In the unique factorization domain $\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$, the exponent of the prime $X$ in $Q^2$ is even, whereas its exponent in $XY$ is $1$. Thus no such $Q$ exists.

Moreover, if $\deg Q\le87$, then $Q^2-XY$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $174$. If it vanished identically on more than $174$ lines through the origin, any nonzero homogeneous part would vanish on more projective directions than its degree permits. Thus it can vanish identically on at most $174$ such lines.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $B(X,Y,Z)=Z^2-XY\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y,Z]$, with variable weights $(1,1,87)$. Then $B$ is primitive as a polynomial in $Z$, irreducible, squarefree, and of weighted degree $174$. There are $73730$ distinct lines through $(0,0)$, each admitting a parameterization $(X,Y)=tv_L$ and a polynomial $P_L(t)$ of degree at most $1$ such that $P_L(0)=0$ and $B(tv_L,P_L(t))\equiv0$. There is no $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ satisfying $B(X,Y,Q(X,Y))=0$.
lemmas.title: Singular pencil

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Let $n=147458$, and let $k_x$ be the number of incident lines whose labels are accepted at $x$. Any two accepted lines through $x$ have equal label values at their intersection because both values equal $f(x)$. Consequently,

$$C\ge\frac{\mathbb{E}_x[\binom{k_x}{2}]}{\binom{n}{2}}.$$

The mean of $k_x$ is $\alpha n$. Convexity of $k\mapsto k(k-1)$ gives

$$\mathbb{E}_x[k_x(k_x-1)]\ge \alpha n(\alpha n-1),$$

and hence

$$C\ge\alpha(\alpha n-1)/(n-1)=\alpha((147458)\alpha-1)/147457.$$

At the verified record, set $u=7099751645463$ and $S=10^{13}$, so $\alpha=u/S$. The guaranteed lower bound is

$$u(147458u-S)/(147457S^2)=0.5040633378625397\ldots.$$

This lower bound is less than $101/200$, as certified exactly by

$$101\cdot147457\cdot S^2-200u(147458u-S)=2762347776069871008518383199600>0.$$
lemmas.statement_markdown:
Let a point table $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$ and degree-at-most-$87$ affine-line labels have acceptance $\alpha$. Let $C$ be the fraction of unordered nonparallel line pairs whose labels agree at their intersection. Then

$$C\ge\alpha((147458)\alpha-1)/147457.$$
lemmas.title: Pair consistency

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Take a random bipartite graph with $147457$ vertices in each part, including each edge independently with probability $51/100$. The expected edge density is $51/100$. Since the target density $101/200$ is smaller by $1/200$, Chebyshev's inequality gives probability at most

$$10000/147457^2$$

that the graph has density below $101/200$.

The expected number of copies of $K_{88,25}$ is at most

$$147457^{113}(51/100)^{2200}.$$

Since $147457<2^{18}$ and $2200=22\cdot100$, the exact certificate

$$100^{22}-2^{21}\cdot51^{22}=22701016461206007127309440037081676825755648>0$$

implies $(51/100)^{2200}<2^{-2100}$. Therefore the expected number of copies is less than

$$2^{18\cdot113}2^{-2100}=2^{2034-2100}=2^{-66}.$$

By Markov's inequality, the probability that a copy exists is below $2^{-66}$. Since

$$10000/147457^2+2^{-66}<1,$$

there is a graph satisfying both required properties.

Thus the pair-density guarantee in $P11$, by itself, cannot force even $25$ common neighbors for $88$ anchors, whereas the anchored configuration in $P7$ requires at least $175$. This is an incidence-level obstruction and does not assert that every such graph is realizable by a complete low-degree line table.
lemmas.statement_markdown: There exists a bipartite graph with $147457$ vertices in each part, edge density at least $101/200$, and no subgraph isomorphic to $K_{88,25}$.
lemmas.title: Density obstruction

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Fix the origin and choose one nonzero representative $v_D$ for each of the $147458$ projective directions $D$. Independently for every $D$, choose a uniform polynomial $S_D$ of degree at most $86$. Define

$$f(tv_D)=tS_D(t)$$

for nonzero points on the ray and set $f(0)=0$. This definition is consistent because every nonzero point lies on a unique ray through the origin. Every pencil line through the origin carries the exact degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial $tS_D(t)$.

Let $Q$ have total degree at most $87$ and satisfy $Q(0)=0$. On each direction write $Q(tv_D)=tT_D(t)$. For any fixed five directions, the image rank of the map $Q\mapsto(T_D)$ is

$$\sum_{k=1}^{87}\min\{5,k+1\}=2+3+4+84\cdot5=429,$$

inside a target space of dimension $5\cdot87=435$. Hence the probability that some $Q$ matches all five complete rays is $147457^{-6}$. A union bound over the choices of five directions costs at most

$$\binom{147458}{5}147457^{-6}.$$

For a fixed $Q$, let $W_D$ count matching nonzero points on a ray that is not completely matched by $Q$, and set $W_D=0$ on a completely matched ray. Exact subset counting, separately for $Q(0)=0$ and $Q(0)\ne0$, gives

$$\mathbb{E}[2^{W_D}]<\sum_{s\ge0}1/s!=e<11/4.$$

For fixed $Q$, these variables are independent across directions. Markov's inequality and a union bound over the $147457^{3916}$ total-degree-at-most-$87$ polynomials give

$$\Pr[\exists Q:\sum_DW_D\ge2\cdot147458]<147457^{3916}(11/16)^{147458}.$$

Because $147457<2^{18}$ and $(11/16)^2=121/256<1/2$, this is less than

$$2^{18\cdot3916-73729}=2^{-3241}.$$

Also,

$$\binom{147458}{5}147457^{-6}<32/(120\cdot147457)<1/2.$$

The two bad-event bounds sum to less than $1$. Therefore some deterministic choice of the polynomials $S_D$ has the following properties simultaneously for every $Q$: at most four rays are completely matched, and the remaining nonzero matches total fewer than $2\cdot147458$.

If $Q(0)=0$, its number of matches is less than

$$1+4(147457-1)+2(147457+1)=6\cdot147457-1.$$

If $Q(0)\ne0$, the number is smaller. Thus every total-degree-at-most-$87$ polynomial satisfies $\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)<6/147457$.

Label all $147458$ pencil lines through the origin exactly by their polynomials $tS_D(t)$. On every other affine line, choose $88$ distinct points and interpolate the values of $f$ there with a polynomial of degree at most $87$. The resulting acceptance is at least

$$1/147457+(1-1/147457)(88/147457)=(89\cdot147457-88)/147457^2=13123585/21743566849.$$

Finally,

$$29\cdot147457-88=4276165>0,$$

so $6/147457$ is strictly less than one tenth of the displayed acceptance lower bound. For every $\varepsilon$ in the stated interval, the tables have acceptance at least $\varepsilon$ and agreement below $\varepsilon/10$ against every permitted global polynomial.
lemmas.statement_markdown:
There exist a point table $f:\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}\to\mathbb{F}_{147457}$ and degree-at-most-$87$ labels on all affine lines such that

$$\operatorname{Pass}\ge13123585/21743566849$$

and $\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)<6/147457$ for every $Q\in\mathbb{F}_{147457}[X,Y]$ of total degree at most $87$. Consequently, for every

$$\varepsilon\in[60/147457,\,13123585/21743566849],$$

the tables satisfy $\operatorname{Pass}\ge\varepsilon$ and $\operatorname{Agr}(f,Q)<\varepsilon/10$ for every such $Q$.
lemmas.title: Pencil counterexample

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Exact cross multiplication gives

$$145640\cdot10^{13}-147457\cdot7099751645463=409491921614962409>0.$$

The denominators are positive, so $145640/147457>7099751645463/10^{13}$. Because a lower soundness threshold is better, the direct threshold proved in $P6$ is weaker than the verified record.
lemmas.statement_markdown: Let $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dir}}=145640/147457$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}=7099751645463/10^{13}$. Then $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dir}}>\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rec}}$, so the direct soundness threshold does not improve the live doubly verified record.
lemmas.title: Benchmark comparison

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Put $P=147457^2=21743566849$, $\Lambda=147457(147457+1)=21743714306$, $a=22796$, and $b=35928$. Stop a valid deletion order when either exactly $b$ point vertices or exactly $a$ line vertices first remain. If the point boundary occurs first, arbitrary line deletions down to $a$ remaining lines are valid because every remaining line meets at most $b$ remaining points. The symmetric argument applies if the line boundary occurs first.

Charge every earlier edge to its first deleted endpoint. If $I$ is the number of residual incidences between the $b$ points and the $a$ lines, then
$$
|E(G)|\le a(P-b)+b(\Lambda-a)+I.
$$
For each boundary point $x$, let $r_x$ be the number of the $a$ lines through it. Since two affine lines meet in at most one point,
$$
\sum_x\binom{r_x}{2}\le\binom{a}{2}=259817410.
$$
For fixed $\sum_x r_x=I$, discrete convexity minimizes the left-hand side when the values $r_x$ differ by at most one. If
$$
I=4338790=120b+27430,
$$
that minimum is
$$
b\binom{120}{2}+27430\cdot120=259817520>259817410.
$$
Thus $I\le4338789$, and consequently
$$
|E(G)|\le aP+b\Lambda-2ab+4338789=1276872883785185.
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown: In the fixed instance $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$, let $G$ be a subgraph of the affine point-line incidence graph of $\mathbb{F}_{147457}^{2}$. If iteratively deleting point vertices of degree at most $22796$ and line vertices of degree at most $35928$ empties $G$, then $G$ has at most $1276872883785185$ edges.
lemmas.title: Geometric first-core bound

lemmas.proof_markdown:
For a point set $X$, let $n_L=|X\cap L|$. Ordered-pair counting gives
$$
\sum_L n_L=(p+1)|X|,
\qquad
\sum_L n_L^2=|X|^2+p|X|.
$$
With $a_X=|X|/p^2$, it follows that
$$
\sum_L(n_L-a_Xp)^2=p^3a_X(1-a_X).
$$
Centering the indicator of a line set and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields
$$
I(X,T)\le\frac{|X||T|}{p}+\sqrt{p|X||T|}.
$$
Let $x$ and $n$ be the point and line counts of the first core, and set $m_0=\min(x,n)$ and $M_0=\max(x,n)$. The minimum-degree conditions give at least $22797M_0$ retained edges. Hence
$$
22797M_0\le\frac{m_0M_0}{p}+\sqrt{pm_0M_0}.
$$
After division by $M_0$,
$$
22797\le\frac{m_0}{p}+\sqrt{\frac{pm_0}{M_0}}\le\frac{m_0}{p}+\sqrt p<\frac{m_0}{p}+385.
$$
Therefore
$$
m_0>p(22797-385),
$$
and integrality gives
$$
x,n\ge p(22797-385)+1=3304806285.
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown: In the fixed instance $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$, every nonempty first core with point minimum degree $22797$ and line minimum degree $35929$ has at least $3304806285$ vertices on each side.
lemmas.title: First-core support

lemmas.proof_markdown:
Select every line vertex independently with probability
$$
\theta=\frac{22691}{455920000}.
$$
Fix a first-core line and retain exactly $35929$ of its accepted neighbors. Each retained point has at least $22796$ alternative first-core line neighbors. The alternative-line sets belonging to distinct points of the fixed line are disjoint, so their coverage indicators are independent.

The coverage probability of each retained point is at least
$$
1-(1-\theta)^{22796}>1-\exp\left(-\frac{22691}{20000}\right)>\rho,
\qquad
\rho=\frac{1696083}{2500000}.
$$
The last comparison is certified exactly by
$$
S_{11}=\sum_{j=0}^{11}\frac{(22691/20000)^j}{j!}
$$
and
$$
(1-\rho)S_{11}-1>0.
$$
Hoeffding's inequality bounds the probability that at most $D=23712$ retained points are covered by
$$
\exp\left(-\frac{2(\rho\cdot35929-D)^2}{35929}\right).
$$
Here
$$
\rho\cdot35929-D=\frac{1658566107}{2500000}
$$
and
$$
\frac{2(\rho\cdot35929-D)^2}{35929}
=
\frac{49}{2}+\frac{1445725743971}{5909375000000000}.
$$
Since
$$
e>\sum_{j=0}^{6}\frac1{j!}=\frac{1957}{720}
$$
and
$$
1957^{49}>4\Lambda^2 720^{49},
$$
the union failure probability over all first-core lines is less than $\Lambda\exp(-49/2)<1/2$.

For the selected family $R$, its mean satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}|R|\le\theta\Lambda
=
\frac{246693310658723}{227960000}.
$$
Writing $R_0=1083220$, the gap is
$$
R_0-\theta\Lambda
=
\frac{237520541277}{227960000}.
$$
Cantelli's inequality, with the failure bound maximized at this upper bound on the mean, gives
$$
\Pr[|R|\le1083219]
\ge
\frac{56416007528519060790729}{112652214626281555870729}
>
\frac12.
$$
The cover-good and size-good probabilities sum to more than one, so some deterministic family satisfies both properties. Finally, $D+1$ covered points of a fixed line require $D+1$ distinct selected alternative lines. Thus
$$
23713=D+1\le|R|\le1083219.
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown: In the fixed instance $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$, every first core has a set $R$ of line vertices satisfying $23713\le |R|\le1083219$ such that every first-core line has at least $23713$ accepted points covered by lines in $R$.
lemmas.title: Sparse reaching family

lemmas.proof_markdown:
The number of monomials of weight at most $D=23712$ is
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{272}\binom{D-87k+2}{2}=25686375897.
$$
Every selected line imposes at most $D+1=23713$ homogeneous linear conditions. Since $|R|\le1083219$, the number of conditions is at most
$$
1083219\cdot23713=25686372147,
$$
leaving a surplus of $3750$. Hence a nonzero interpolant of weighted degree at most $D$ exists.

A nonzero interpolant independent of $Z$ would be a bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $D$ vanishing formally on at least $D+1$ distinct lines, contrary to KTZ Lemma 2.5. Thus the interpolant depends on $Z$. Its degree in $Z$ is at most $272<147457$, so its derivative with respect to $Z$ is nonzero.

Let $S$ contain every graph point of every selected line. Among the nonzero polynomials vanishing on $S$ with nonzero derivative with respect to $Z$, choose one of minimum weighted degree and call it $A$. KTZ Lemma 2.3 makes $A$ squarefree. Its weighted degree is at most $D<147457$. Therefore its $147457$ pointwise zeros on each selected line imply the formal identity
$$
A(L(t),P_L(t))=0.
$$
lemmas.statement_markdown: In the fixed instance $m=2$, $p=147457$, and $d=87$, give $X,Y,Z$ weights $1,1,87$.
